speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, If I can have the unanimous consent of the House for the proceeding, I should like again to draw attention to the desirability of having an interim supply bill. On the assumption that there will be no objection to my doing so I may say that the procedure which I had asked the House to take yesterday was, I am assured, in accord with the established practice of the House. It had been contemplated that we should move concurrence in all the votes already passed in supply and then ask for a vote of one-sixth of the remainder. Hon. gentlemen opposite suggested that the motion for one-sixth should apply to the concurrence as well. As a matter of precedent, I think my own contention was the right one. But I am much more concerned to get the business done than to stand on any ceremony, and therefore I have asked the officials to prepare the resolutions so that they shall apply to one-sixth of the concurrence as well as to one-sixth of the votes. I have discussed this matter with the hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) who concurs in the motion I am now making. If the House is content that I shall take this course, I therefore move that the Speaker leave the chair and the House go into Committee of Supply in order that I may move the first resolution.
Motion agreed to and the House went into Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to a return brought down yesterday by the Minister of Labour. In the first place, I draw his attention to the fact that the return does not comply with his. undertaking of the 23rd and his statement of the return yesterday. Obviously it does not contain all the correspondence. It does not contain the first communication to Mr. Pacaud, now of the High Commissioner's office, asking him to represent Canada. That would be an important element of the return, as it contains the instructions. I would point out also that the request which finally resulted in the appointment of Mrs. Carruthers was received, not late, as stated by the minister, but on the 6th of March, the meeting not being held until the 10th of April, and that the communication asking for Mr. Pacaud was not by cable, as stated by the minister, but by letter. It would appear, therefore, that there was plenty of time for another appointment. But I wish to impress upon the minister the fact that the return is obviously incomplete, possibly the most important letter of all not being included.

The right hon. gentleman is entirely right. The letter to Mr. Pacaud dated March 6, which was the date on which the agenda of the next meeting of the governing body was received, is regarded as a communication that it would be inadvisable under the circumstances to lay on the Table. I shall be glad, however, to let my right hon friend read it.

I do not know why I should have special privileges. It is a letter giving the position of the government in relation to this convention, and, I presume, giving instructions. Surely that should not come under the category of secret diplomacy.

Not at all. It was written by the Minister of Labour expressing the view of the Department of Labour as to

British Columbia Fisheries

what was desired in such representation as might be undertaken by a properly qualified person at the sessions of the governing body. There is nothing improper in that communication. My right hon. friend can read it, though, and judge for himself.

I do not suggest, I never thought of suggesting, that there was anything improper; but as it is the view of the Department of Labour, I do not know why it should be secret. However, that is the minister's position.

On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. J. A. CLARK (Burrard) asked leave, under rule 39, to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the giving of a pledge in December last by the Department of Marine and Fisheries to the salmon canners of British Columbia respecting the regulations and conditions under which that industry might be conducted during the season of 1923, and the announcement in March 1923 by the same department that such pledge is not to be honoured, with immediate resultant loss to those engaged in such industry, who relied on the sanctity of the pledge so given.

The hon. member has followed the procedure and the practice with regard to motions of this kind. Under rule 39, subsection 4, the mover hands a written statement of the matter poposed to be discussed to the Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the House to proceed. The motion is certainly drafted as it should be. I must confess that I have a doubt as to the question whether or not the matter is one of urgent public importance. It would certainly be one of importance in the county which I have. the honour to represent, the county of Gaspe, and I know it is a matter of importance in British Columbia. Is it a matter of urgent public importance throughout the whole Dominion? Perhaps so. Indeed, I am inclined to believe it may be a matter of urgent public importance, affecting as it does a large industry, prices, and so on. Therefore I would give the hon. member the benefit of the doubt.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
May I say a word? I know this motion is not debatable, but I
[Mr. Murdock.!
wish to point out that my hon. friend advised me at a quarter past two to-day-I met him on the way to the dining-room-that he was going to bring up this matter this afternoon. I immediately asked for all the documents papers and records, but they have not yet arrived. I would ask my hon. friend to postpone this matter at least until to-morrow.

It is true I met the minister around noon and spoke to him about the matter, but I had tried during the morning to notify him. I left word at his department and told him what I proposed to do. But the fact is this-

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman but I should like to conclude the remarks I was making to the House in support of the stand I intend to take. The matter must be not only of public importance but also of urgency. On the question of urgency, the hon. gentleman states in his motion that the pledge alleged to have been given by the Department of Marine and Fisheries if not honoured would result in immediate loss to those engaged in this industry. Under the circumstances, therefore, I believe that I should favour the broad principle of freedom of speech and let the hon. gentleman air his grievance, if he has one. before the House.

Last summer a Fisheries Commission was appointed to investigate the fisheries of British Columbia. During the time of its investigations the Department of Marine and Fisheries carried on negotiatons with the salmon canners of British Columbia, and in June last the department assured the canners that irrespective of the decision arrived at by the commission no change would be made in the number of licenses issued, other than white and Indian licenses, beyond the 10 per cent reduction laid down by the department. In December last the Fisheries Commission filed its preliminary report, which recommended a 40 per cent reduction of these licenses. The canners thereupon made an inquiry of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) who sent this telegram to the Salmon Canners' Association:
No action will be taken on commission's report that will affect next season. Therefore existing regulations and policy including reduction in Oriental licenses decided upon last June will govern industry next year.
That reply was dated December, 22, 1922.
Who signed it?

I rise as the seconder of the motion. There is no doubt that this matter is one of great importance to British Columbia. I also have had some communications with the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) regarding this matter. The salmon industry is one of the largest in Canada. It is one in which the co-operation of the proper department of the government is most necessary owing to the serious competition which the industry has to face from the United States, particularly the state of Washington across the line, and as the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) has mentioned, from Siberia also.
It seems to me, in a word, that the report of this commission, on the merits or demerits of which I do not propose to make any remarks at the present time, is not the question involved here, but the simple question of abiding by the undertaking of responsible members of the government so that business men, laying out their plans for the year-as cannery men must do-and making their expenditures and their arrangements, will be able to do so knowing that the governmental regulations under which they work will be of a kind consistent with the plans which they have formed. There may be some explanation which the minister has to offer; and I would urge upon the government, and upon hon. members, that this matter be dealt with
British Columbia Fisheries

dispassionately and fairly, and that the great industries of the country be not hampered or handicapped by action of this kind. There is no reason why they should be; there is nothing to be gained by changing an arrangement or undertaking such as that. Even the political aspect of the question is not one that would commend itself to a minister of the Crown under such circumstances. I trust that the government will see its way clear to make such adjustments, conforming to their own original declarations, as will give justice and fair treatment to those interested in the business.

I am very glad indeed that both the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) have made such short speeches on such an important question as the fisheries of British Columbia. I will, therefore, endeavour to make my own remarks brief although I have been so loaded up with material on this very important matter during the past six months that I am afraid I shall continue talking all the afternoon and all the evening unless somebody pulls my coat tails as a signal for me to sit down. Now, Sir, if I understand the remarks of the hon. member for Burrard he finds no fault with the decision arrived at by the British Columbia Fisheries Commission, which was composed of members representing all the groups in this House.
I reserve my remarks on that point.

We will be very glad if the hon. member at some time in the future, will discuss the report of that commission; speaking for my fellow commissioners and myself we would be very glad indeed to see that report discussed. However, if I followed my hon. friend's remarks correctly, and also those of the hon. member for Vancouver South, there seems to be some difference of opinion as to whether a reduction of 10 per cent, or a reduction of 40 per cent, should be put into force in the case of Japanese licenses-
No, that is wrong.

Just let me finish my sentence- and because the department finally decided to. put the 40 per cent reduction into effect, my hon. friends argue that thereby the industry would suffer very seriously. Personally I do not think there is going to be any serious handicap placed on the canneries of British Columbia by reason of the fact that the government has put a 40 per cent reduction into effect.

If my hon. friend seriously intends to discuss the merits of the question he is not doing so. May I direct his attention to the fact that we make no argument with respect to the reduction of the licenses. The point we are emphasizing is the undertaking given by the government, which has nothing whatever to do with the report in question.

What the hon. gentleman says may be quite correct, but if I correctly understood the argument of his colleague and himself they claimed that the government at a certain time decided to make a reduction of 10 per cent, and later reversed that decision and made a reduction of 40 per cent, and their complaint is that the government should have stuck to the 10 per cent reduction because their later action is seriously affecting the canneries of British Columbia.
No, that was not the argument.

That is just exactly what my hon. friends said and nothing else. The whole thing boils itself down to this, if I understood both hon. gentlemen correctly, that due to the fact that the government, or some official in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, sent word to the fishery interests in British Columbia that a reduction of 10 per cent was to be made, and that afterwards another decision was arrived at and a reduction of 40 per cent effected, those interests are going to be seriously handicapped and affected in 1923, with the result that the men who operate the canneries are going to lose a large amount of money during that year. I am not trying to say that these two hon. gentlemen are in favour of a lower reduction in Japanese licenses; I am not arguing that at all. If that is their fear I will put their minds at rest right now. All I want to argue is this: Whether the department did or did not change their policy with regard to the percentage of licenses that should go into effect in 1923, nevertheless the canneries of British Columbia are not going to be seriously handicapped or affected by that policy. Now, what are the circumstances? It is a fact that salmon fishing in British Columbia does not start until some time in June-the 15th, of June if I remember correctly. Consequently even at this late day, although the 40 per cent policy has been adopted now for over a month, the fact remains that the canners have about five months in which to make their arrangements. Now, what arrangements have they to make? One hon. gentleman said they are going to lose hundreds of thousands of dollars.

British Columbia Fisheries
May I ask Ihc hon. gentleman what he means by saying that the Banners have five months in which to make their arrangements?

If the hon. gentleman will take into consideration the time from the date when it was decided by the department to put the 40 per cent reduction into effect it will not be very much less than five months.
But the department decided to put the reduction into effect before they received the report. The report was filed on the 28th February.
There was an interim report which asked the government to decrease the renewal licenses to Japanese by 40 per cent.
That was on the 23rd December and the department gave its pledge that they were not going to consider it.

Quite possibly. I am not arguing that the department did not change their policy, but evidently the members of the British Columbia Fisheries Commission were able ' to convince them that it was the right and proper thing to do, not only in the interests of the fisheries of British Columbia but in the interests of the people of the province as a whole; and as one of the commissioners I certainly think the department did the right and proper th.rng when they decided to accept the report ol the commission in that regard and reducing Japanese licenses 40 per cent. Now, Sir, the hon. member for Burrard said that the British Columbia canners had signed contracts for labour and material. Well, even if they have done so-
And made advances.

And made advances. To
whom? To Japanese. I hope my hon. friends will not press that part of the question. It is quite possible, as he said, that advances are made to fishermen; but the only advances which the canners make at this early date, or at the time my hon friend said they were made in December, is when they go to the Japanese bosses and engage a certain number of Japanese for the next season. Now there is nothing to prevent the canners from getting other fishermen; they have five months in which they can do it. There is absolutely no .reason why, if (.he canners want to employ white fishermen they cannot go and get them. I say it is about time-in British Columbia or anywhere else-that white people should be employed in the fishing business, and the canners ought to go out and get help of that kind.

Does the hon. gentleman seriously contend that it makes one bit of difference, so far as the honour of the government is concerned, whether the moneys were advaned to Japanese, Chinese, Hottentots or anybody else? If relying on the pledge of the government the canners set out on a certain business course and now the government takes the ground from under them and subjects them to a loss of several thousand dollars, what difference does it make to whom the advances are made?

I am glad my hon. friend has set the loss at several thousand dollars. The hon. member for Burrard said the loss would amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars. I am very doubtful whether the canners have advanced any money to the fishermen in British Columbia up to the present date-very doubtful indeed. It is true, of course, that the canners have to make certain arrangements such as buying cans, tin plate, boxes and other supplies for the fisheries; but what difference is it going to make to the canners of British Columbia whether the reduction in Japanese licenses is 10 per cent or 40 per cent as regards the quantity of supplies which they have to buy for the 1923 fisheries? If my hon. friend will read the statistics of the British Columbia fisheries he will see that in certain years when there has been a smaller number employed than in previous years, there has been a larger catch. Therefore, the man engaged in fishing in British Columbia cannot know the quantity of boxes or other supplies he will require from time to time. He has to prepare himself to handle a large quantity of fish, and, consequently, it is impossible for him to argue that because a certain per cent reduction in the number of licenses issued to orientals is taking place the canners are going to be seriously affected in that regard. I do not wish to argue that the department is infallible. It is as liable to make mistakes as other people, and I might say that perhaps the Department of Marine and Fisheries makes more mistakes than some other departments, but that is no reason why it should be condemned in this matter, and I do not think it is a matter of grave public importance to be discussed this afternoon or that the House should be prevented from going into Committee of Supply. This matter might have been discussed when the fishery estimates were before the House. There would have been ample time to discuss it then, and the only reason I can see why it is brought up now is to make political capital against the department and the government. I contend the British Columbia fisheries are
1544	COMMONS
British Columbia Fisheries
not going to be affected in the least by the fact that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) has said that one of the officials of the department sent a telegram in December last to British Columbia saying that the 10 per cent reduction was going into effect. I think I can say truthfully that, perhaps, I have received more correspondence regarding this matter and other matters connected with the British Columbia fisheries before and since our interim and final reports were filed, than any other man in this House. I have received telegrams and letters upholding the views of the commission, thanking the commission for recommending the 40 per cent reduction, not only from the fishermen of British Columbia, not only from citizens of British Columbia, not themselves interested in the fisheries, but also from gentlemen interested in the fisheries. I do not think there is any very great concern in British Columbia about the 40 per cent reduction, or the loss it will entail upon the canners when it goes into effect. In fact I have a telegram from a prominent canner; I just happened to find it a moment ago. The telegram is
4 p.m. addressed to me and quotes a telegram sent to the minister part of which is as follows:
We urge your department to put in force the recommendation of the Duff report and immediate application of exclusion of Japanese from seine operations or working on same. Any variation from this, such as 40 per cent reduction, will cause endless worry to those who use whites and Indians and will only lead to endless trouble in the future; there is plenty of good white men and Indians for this work and our company have not for years used any Japs on either herring or salmon seines.

Who is that from?
Mr. DUFF 1 I will give the name if the hon. member wants it, but perhaps the gentleman who wrote it would not want his name mentioned. I will show it to the hon. member, if he wishes to see it. It is from a prominent canner and is addressed to me. He quotes a telegram which he sent to the minister.

I thought it was from the
new Minister of Fisheries.

I did not catch that remark. Now, Sir, the hon. member for Vancouver South referred to the fact that the Canadian canners on the Fraser river had to compete with the American fishermen and canners, and for that reason, I understood him to say, he did not think it was right for the department to change their decision. Everybody knows that the Americans do not employ Japanese in their operations on the

Fraser river, and consequently his argument falls to the ground.
I do not think it is necessary for me to discuss this matter any further. All I wish to say is that I think the Department of Marine and Fisheries were fully justified in accepting the report of the British Columbia Fisheries Commission. Nobody is going to be hurt in any possible way, so far as we can see. We went into the matter just as fully as it was possible in the four weeks prior to the date upon which we signed our report. Every member of that commission, practically for every day, was discussing what was best to put in our report, and we gave a great deal of time and thought to this matter, and, with the exception of one of the members of the commission who did not quite concur with us in regard to the 40 per cent reduction, we were practically unanimous on all the other phases of the questions discussed. But I say, from my knowledge of the matter, that the cannere of British Columbia are not going to be affected. I do not need to discuss the report, but I wish to say that in that report a great many concessions are made to the canners-more than any other commission ever gave them. I do not think the canners will say that I am not favourable to them and that I do not want to see them get a square deal. I think it is practically second nature to me to be interested in the fisheries of this country. From the time, almost, that, I drew breath I have been interested, and my people before me, in the fishing business, and from the standpoint of the fish merchant; so that any particular sympathy which I would have would naturally be with the men who have to invest large sums of money in this industry and who sometimes do not get very large returns. Consequently, I say that the commission did not arrive at its decision with a view of doing anything which would be in any way detrimental to the interests of the canners. We had all these representations made to us by the canners. We were told that the department had first thought of making a 10 per cent reduction. They told us their business would be affected by it. We made every possible investigation we could into the matter before we arrived at our decision, and I think hon. members will agree with me that, with the composition of the commission, the decision we arrived at is in the interests of British Columbia, and in the interests not only of the fishermen but of the men who have their money invested in that industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
It is indeed of some

British Columbia Fisheries
interest that we should be attacked for having been too harsh towards a certain class of orientals in British Columbia. There is something queer about this question. There are members who want to exclude the orientals, except those whom they employ themselves, or who are employed by their friends. It reminds me of an incident in my early parliamentary career in this House. The House had been seized with the very question of oriental immigration to British Columbia, and gentlemen had been vehement in their denunciations of the government for allowing these people to come into Canada. After four or five speeches along that line I remember one of their cleverest members of the House at that time, the late Mr. Ralph Smith, in a speech he delivered said: "Now, I want to know who among the gentlemen who have just spoken does not employ orientals in his own personal business?" And he added, "Don't all talk at once." Nobody answered. Well, last year we had a very interesting discussion in this House when a similar motion was considered, and a dark picture indeed was painted of the dangers that were menacing British Columbia. My hon. friend who is moving the adjournment this afternoon made a speech himself, and I may be allowed to cite just a few words from it. He said:
I submit we must take our stand on this question and take it at once. We must be firm; we must be clear and definite in our policy. If we do that we shall be respected; if we do not, we shall be treated contemptuously.
And the hon. member concluded by saying:
It is a matter for the white race, particularly the Canadian white race, to consider and deal with now before the menace becomes such that our whole country is more seriously threatened than it is to-day. I am in entire agreement with my fellow members from British Columbia, and I sincerely hope that the House will take the matter firmly in hand without delay.
Well, I thought that perhaps I had taken the matter somewhat firmly in hand recently, and I am now faced with the criticism of my hon. friend who says I have violated solemn pledges and should issue more licenses to Japanese in British Columbia. Now, Mr. Speaker, what are the facts of the case? A committee was appointed to study the question of the fisheries in British Columbia. And with the consent of the House, indeed at the unanimous demand of the House, a commission was appointed composed of members of that committee to go and hear witnesses and investigate all matters concerning the British Columbia fisheries and make a report. Members were selected from every side of the House and I may give the list of them. This commission was composed of the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), who was chairman, the
member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), the member for Hants (Mr. Martell), the member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie), the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), and the member for Skeena (Mr. Stork). Four of the members of that commission are representing British Columbia in this House. The commission investigated every matter concerning the fisheries of that province; they heard witnesses in various parts of British Columbia; and while their labours were still uncompleted they sent in an interim report to the department recommending that the number of licenses of all kinds issued to other than white British subjects and Indians in 1923 be 40 per cent less than the number issued in 1922. They stated that they were still considering the subject and that the final report would be filed later on. At that time, in December last, I was away, but I do not want to evade any responsibility; I accept the full responsibility for everything that was done in the department. The officers of the department, however, said that taking into account the fact that the report was only of an interim character and that there was no finality in the finding of the commission at that time, this provision should not apply to the next season. I admit that this was done.
Was it not the deputy who said that?

Yes; nobody said it was not the deputy. The commission continued its work until the 28th of February, and it filed another report in which I find the following on page 8:
The commissioners were absolutely unanimous on all points dealt with in their interim recommendations, with the exception of the one dealing with the closing of Fraser river to sockeye fishing for five years. Two of the commissioners differed from the majority, as will appear later, on the question as to how overfishing was to be prevented after the closed period.
The representations that have been made by the various interests concerned in the British Columbia fisheries, as well as the objections raised by certain officials of the department since the publication of the commission's interim report have been carefully considered by the commissioners before the writing of their final report. Our conclusions and recommendations hereinafter set forth have therefore been reached and agreed upon in the full light of the said further recommendations.
On page 13 the recommendation of the committee appears as follows:
We therefore again recommend and most strongly urge-
And mark, they cay previously that it is in the light of the knowledge they had of what had passed between the department and the interests concerned that they make their recommendation.
British Columbia Fisheries

-that the number of licenses of all kinds, except trolling licenses, issued to other than white British Columbia subjects and Indians in 1923 be 40 per cent less than the number issued in 1922.
Now, one of the members of the commission, my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), did not agree with the recommendation in so far as it reduced by 40 per cent the number of licenses to be issued. He wanted the reduction to be only 25 per cent.
That referred only to the waters of the Skeena and the Naas, for reasons which I gave to the House; it had no reference to the waters below, where the majority of the fishermen are employed.
Except in the area to which my hon. friend refers, I think he was in favour of a reduction by 40'per cent.
Yes, decidedly so.

But even in the district of which my hon. friend made an exception, recommending a reduction of only 25 per cent, he agreed with all the other commissioners that the reduction should take effect this year for the season of 1923. So that a commission composed of members of this House representing all sides, four of whom represented British Columbia, considered the question, knowing everything that had passed, and recommended and insisted very urgently that this reduction should be made at once.

Does the minister say
that they knew of the government's pledge of December?

They practically say so:
In the full light of the said further representations.
Does the minister say that they were informed of the government's pledge, or that their report had any relation in the world to that pledge?

I do not know whether they saw the telegram which my hon. friend construes as a pledge. I must draw his attention to the fact that their recommendation was based on an interim report, while the present decision of the department is based on the final report unanimously recommending and insisting that the department make its decision effective this year. And that is why I have issued instructions accordingly. Now, Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to think that anyone will suffer by reason of that decision. Is it to be said that the white fishermen of British Columbia cannot do their work?

Has the minister any
reason to doubt the positive assertion of the canners' association?

I have had representations not only from the canners but from members of the House of Commons and, as well, from members of that commission. And my hon. friend himself speaks violently in this House against the danger of employing Japanese fishermen. My hon. friend and Ins associates last year said that British Columbia was confronted with the danger of all its fisheries going to the Japanese. Yet directly the very first step is taken by this department to avert the danger by reducing the licenses to Japanese fishermen, I am accused by those hon. gentlemen of having broken faith with the salmon canners of British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker-
Order. The hon. member can only speak by leave of the hon. gentleman who has the floor.

I hesitate to rise a second time, but the hon. minister has touched upon an important point. May I ask him if anything which either the hon. member for Bur-rard (Mr. Clark) or I stated can give him the slightest excuse-
That is a matter of argument.
-to say that we alluded to the reduction of Japanese licenses or the oriental question at all?
Order.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker I may say that the licenses will not be issued until next month. And here is a letter of which my hon. friend for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) received a copy. In answer to my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) I wrote him on March 14th, 1923, as follows:
My dear Mr. Stevens,-I have your note of the 12th inst., with which was enclosed a telegram addressed to you by the B. C. Salmon Packers Association protesting against the proposal of the department to reduce the number of licenses to Japanese fishermen and asking for sympathetic consideration of the same by me.
You will recall that the special fisheries commission appointed to inquire into fishery matters in British Columbia during the past season, submitted an interim report in the month of September last, recommending inter alia the reduction of licenses to fishermen other than whites and Indians by 40 per cent. In view of the intimation by the commission that a fuller and final report would follow at a later period, the officials of the department after having given the matter careful consideration concluded not to make effective the recommendations contained in the interim report for the season 1923. The commission has in the meantime completed its investigations and submitted it* final report a few days ago. The commissioners, with Mr. Dickie dissenting, adhere to the recommendations submitted in the interim report to the effect that these licenses should be reduced by 40 per cent. Mr. Dickie,

British Columbia Fisheries
in a minority report recommends that the reduction should not be more than 25 per cent. The commissioners, however, are unanimous in strongly urging that these reductions should be made effective during the present season.
Having regard to the fact that four members representing constituencies in British Columbia sat on this commission, I have felt that I would not be warranted in ignoring their views and declining to make this recommendation effective. It was accordingly decided that the reductions recommended by the majority report should be put into effect this present season and the necessary instructions to that end have already issued. If, however, it appears to you that the general interests of the fisheries are in any way prejudiced by the decision of the department in this regard, the matter might well receive further consideration by the House of Commons Committee on Marine and Fisheries.
Why do not those gentlemen take advantage of the committee that has [DOT] been reappointed for this session, and is actually sitting, to discuss this matter? Then should the committee find otherwise than the commission has found, the question will be still open for further consideration.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the issue raised by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) is not by this time thoroughly obscured, it will not be for lack of will or of skill on the part of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr Duff) and of the hon. minister (Mr. Lapointe).
Thank you very much.

What has the House discussed? One would think from the speeches heard from the other side that an appeal had been made by hon. gentlemen behind me against the treatment of Japanese in the province of British Columbia, and urging that more Japanese fishermen be employed, even against the report of the Fisheries Commission that has sat on the subject and made recommendations. No hon. gentleman is so dull as to honestly imagine that that is the issue or that it is relevant to the issue in the remotest way.
The report of the Fisheries Commission everyone understands. We have not all read it. There was an interim report last December ; a final report on the 28th February. The final report, in so far as respects the question of license reduction, was the same as the interim report, which recommended that there be a reduction of Japanese licenses by 40 per cent, effective this year. As to that there is no dispute in the world, and no one in the House has raised the question that that report is good or is bad; no one on this side is objecting to its terms. Then why do hon. members rise and read extracts from speeches delivered last session urging that the Japanese
be excluded? No one recedes from his position in that regard at all.
Now, what is the issue that we are discussing? It is that this government, in response to an inquiry from the British Columbia Salmon Fisheries' Association last December,-an inquiry made by them in order that they might know how to go about their business, making their purchases, making their advances and making their contracts; an inquiry that had to be answered that they might make these preliminary arrangements- gave a definite and unequivocal answer applicable to all this year's business. On the faith of that the British Columbia Salmon Fisheries' Association went to work and made their investments, they hired their men, they made advances to those men, and they made their purchases. After they have thus prepared themselves for their season's work the government comes along in March of this year and says: We will break every pledge we have made to you and will put you back in the position you would have occupied if we had made no pledge to you at all.

If the right hon. gentleman will allow me to correct him? He says that the British Columbia Salmon Canners' Association have hired their men for this season. They could not hire their men until the licenses are issued for this season, and the minister has told us that these licenses will not be issued until next month.
The canners must make their contracts with the men they engage.
They cannot do it.
Of course, in all these matters the member for Lunenburg says the canners have made no losses. Then I wonder what they are complaining about.
I do not know.
The hon. member knows their business a lot better than they do themselves of course. He is the self-constituted president of the exchequer court of the world.

Mr. Speaker, of course the right hon. leader of the Opposition can talk either about sewer gas or angels' wings and impute to me knowledge concerning those things, but it is not fair on his part to say that I claim all knowledge concerning the business of the British Columbia salmon canners. I did not say any such thing, and I am not going to allow him to make any such implication. It is not worthy of him.
British Columbia Fisheries
If the hon. gentleman will admit that the British Columbia salmon canners ought to know their own business better than he knows it-*
They ought to.
Then that ends the argument.
And you might as well sit down, for you do not know anything about it.
Order.

If I sit down now and the hon. gentleman sticks to his admission, the government will have to recede. Now, the minister tries to make the House believe that it was some conditional expression oi view that his department made last December; that there was some expression of opinion by officers of his department that, as this report was merely temporary or interim, they would not feel themselves bound by it, and that in the face of such a conditional expression of view they were quite justified in March of this year in declaring that the final report would be put into effect. Have I misstated in the slightest degree, have I coloured in any way, what the minister said? The minister took good care not to read the undertaking given. This was an undertaking given by his department in response to an inquiry by business men in order that they might know how they should address themselves to the task of making their engagements for this year. If it was not of an}' importance, why would they have made the inquiry? Did they make it just for the fun of sending the telegram? It was because it was of business consequence to them; surely every hon. member will admit that-unless he wants to sit above and in judgment over them and declare that he knows their business better than they. The answer given to the inquiry by the Deputy Minister of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, sent from Ottawa on December 23, was as follows:
No action will be taken on commission's report that will affect next season, therefore existing regulations and policy, including reduction in oriental licenses decided upon last June, will govern industry next year.
A. Johnston,
Deputy Minister.
The minister would lead the House to believe that in the face of that pledge, as direct, as unequivocal, as inescapable a pledge as ever a department gave or ever a man gave, he is free now to tell these people that the regulations will be changed; that there will be not a 10 per cent reduction as fixed for this year, but a 40 per cent reduction, notwithstanding anything they may have done on the faith of that telegram.
Does my right hon. friend say that is too much?
The hon. gentleman is as far from the point as he was at the beginning, and it is hopeless for me to bring him to it.

That is no answer. Is
my right hon. friend afraid of a 40 per cent reduction of Japanese licenses?

If I stand in my place
long enough to bring the commissioner himself to an understanding of the argument, I am afraid I shall impose upon the House. All my efforts so far have been in vain so far as he is concerned, but perhaps that is a credit to my efforts after all. Well, having received that pledge from the department, they ask for confirmation. Here is what they get in reply to their wire:
Your understanding re reduction oriental licenses including trolling correct. Oriental licenses district 2 are to be attached. Reduction to each cannery to be made on number employed this year, preference being given returned soldiers and residents who are bona fide fishermen.
W. A. Found.
Mr. Found, I understand, is Superintendent of Fisheries in the department. So that two leading officers in this department-for whose words and whose undertakings the minister takes responsibility now, and rightly so; he places himself in the position of having signed these telegrams himself-give that assurance to these people, on the faith of which they act. They now come to the government and say. You declare to us that you are not going to abide by that promise; you declare you are going to put into effect a forty per cent reduction. Does the question as to the rightness of the forty per cent reduction come in? Is that an issue now? No hon. gentleman, except possibly one, would ever suggest it was. The other parties to the contract come and say: As the result of the pledge you gave us we have invested hundreds of thousands of dollars; if you break that pledge, we are heavy losers. Now, is it the right of this House to judge whether they are losers or not? Is it the right of the government? I ask the hon. Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) or any member of the government this: Suppose he made a contract with a second party and after the second party had solemnly agreed to the undertaking the minister went ahead to carry it out. Suppose he got his operations well under way and the other party came and said: I cannot abide by the contract; I am going to break it here and now-would he think he had the right or the other party had the right to say whether he was damaged or not? Let us

British Columbia Fisheries
put the government to the test? Will this government undertake to stand liable for the damages to the British Columbia fisheries if they are established before the Exchequer Court? Will the government in this debate undertake to make themselves liable for any damage these men prove they have suffered as the result of the breach of contract by the administration?
Who said it was a breach of contract?

Let them establish it, if they can, before the Exchequer Court of Canada; and if they do, will this government pay the damages? Unless they are ready to make that undertaking, then all the talk they have given us in this debate is just so much froth.
What about your own?

Order. Hon. members must always ask leave of the hon. member who has the floor before interrupting him to put a question. The only interruption provided for in the mass of precedents is sometimes a mild " hear, hear."
In case, Mr. Speaker, there should be any doubt, let me emphasize that your ruling applies even to the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell).
And it doubly applies to the hon. leader of the Opposition.

Let me emphasize before I sit down that this undertaking does not make any reference whatever to any condition ; it is that the commission's report will not be followed for 1923, and it states that throughout that year the regulations that applied last year and the reduction that went into effect as of June of last year will apply for this year. Thus those men were authorized to go ahead on the faith of the pledge of the department. All I want to bring home to the House is this: Those are the terms of the undertaking given, an undertaking which is confirmed by the Superintendent of Fisheries of the department.
Mr. Speaker-
All these things were known to the minister when on the first of March last he told those engaged in the salmon fisheries in British Columbia-
Will the hon. gentleman-
-that the government did not propose to abide by that undertaking.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
I will appeal to the Speaker to bring the hon. member for Hants within the range of the courtesies of parliament.
I wish to ask my right hon. friend a question.
Order.

Perhaps there is some reason for special indulgence to the member for Hants at this particular time. Now, the commission, whether or not any member of it had knowledge of the pledge does not matter, was not asked to report as to what the action of the department should be in relation to any special undertaking of the department; it was asked to report what the policy of the department should be in relation to the conditions in the fisheries industry' of British Columbia. That was what they had to base their finding on, and that alone. So far as I know, no hon. member on this side had knowledge that such a pledge would be or was given. I do know that no hon. member on this side, not even the member of the commission, had knowledge of that pledge. I know that he would have repudiated it, or rather would have stated that no such pledge should have been given; that the minister had no right to give [DOT] it during the pendency of the work of the commission. The report of the commission had no relation to any undertaking of the department, and so far as I know, no hon. member on this side had any knowledge at all of that undertaking. Had he had such knowledge; had the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) or the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) had knowledge of the undertaking, they would not have been justified in having regard to it in making their report. I have not the slightest doubt that they would have paid no attention to the undertaking in determining their duty in relation to the finding of the commission. They had to make a finding on the facts connected with the fisheries industry, what they believed to be best for the industry in British Columbia, and were it not for tins undertaking which the minister should not have given, but which he has given, every one of them would want the report in force, and in force at once. Now it is very easy for us to stand here and say, Oh, these men have not suffered any damage, they can get white men. Everybody knows another man's business usually except that other man himself. We say that aside from pledges no matter whether it is of damage to them
British Columbia Fisheries

or not, the public interest must be considered, and that in the adoption of a general policy as to fisheries there must be a reduction of Japanese licenses. If they are told that in advance and are told to make their arrangements in advance, then, whatever loss there may be, that loss is certainly not chargeable to us; we have done the best we could to make it the least possible. But when they are told the very opposite in advance, that no reduction will be made beyond what was made last year, and they make all their arrangements and all their engagements accordingly, surely it is hardly the part of dignity or of honesty for this government to say: You do not know what you are talking about; you think you have been damaged, but you have not been; we will be the judges whether you are damaged or not-we who at the very moment are admittedly breaking the pledge we gave.	,
That is the case, as I understand it, of the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark), and it seems to mu that the matter of the honour and the good faith of parliament and of government is surely yet of some consequence in this country. I know it has been seriously tampered with of recent months. Hon. members on all sides of this House know that. Hon. members opposite have had their own newspapers calling it in their ears month after month since their conduct has been disclosed to the people of Canada. But still it is of some importance. How can we establish courts of justice through the country in order to compel individuals each with the other to keep his contract if we set the example of violating contracts ourselves, callously and with impunity? The first duty of government is to hold to every engagement it makes-to uphold the honour of the state. If we fail to do that, we will soon find the effects in disrespect for parliament, disrespect for government, and a general lowering of morale throughout the whole country.

As a
member of the fisheries commission I wish to say that I was thoroughly apprised of the notification issued on the 22nd day of December in regard to the proposal to reduce the number of fishing licenses other than to whites and Indians by ten per cent. I did all within my power to have that regulation become non-operative. I was thoroughly convinced that the industry would not suffer if the reduction were made forty per cent.
In connection with the submission of our report, the majority report and the minority report, one thing was sure, that the desire of the whole commission was that the recommendsfMr. Meighon.l
tions should become operative for the year 1923. I presume that I have received copies of all telegrams that have been flooding the capital since this controversy commenced, and I notice that one of the forces used in connection with their argument is the condition in which the canning industry finds itself to-day. Each and every telegram claims that they are suffering loss and are liable to suffer tremendous losses by reason of Siberian competition. The canners, I think, find themselves in this position, that for years they have carried on their operations without hindrance from the people of Canada. They have hired whomsoever they would, with the result that the people whom they have employed for a great number of years in their canneries have learned the cannery business and have gone over to Siberia and established themselves in the canning business there, and they are now competitors in the world's markets. That is one complaint which the cannery people of British Columbia make to-day, of the competition of orientals and foreigners, who, I am free to say, learnt their trade in the shops of the canners of British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak at length. If I got this question right, the issue before the House is this: The department made a pronouncement on the 22nd day of December to the effect that a ten per cent reduction would be made. Recently another pronouncement was made that the reduction would be forty per cent. The hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) claim that this is a breach of faith and that the further reduction should not come into operation. If I understood the member for Vancouver South correctly, he said that much loss would accrue to the cannery people by reason of the increased reduction. The minister has pointed out that even as yet there have been no licenses issued. We have made an alteration apparently between December and March. But the door is still open, as I understand it; modification can still be made, and I would ask the hon. member for Burrard and the hon. member for Vancouver South to put their sincerity to the test and to move here and now that the regulations be altered so as to revert to the ten per cent reduction or whatever other proportion they may deem proper and right.

I would like to begin by confirming the statement made by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) that American canners do not use Japanese in their fishing industry. I

British Columbia Fisheries
believe they use some in their canneries, the same as is done in Canada, but not in the fishing industry.
One of the members from Vancouver made the remark that the cannery men were liable to suffer heavy loss owing to having made big advances to fishermen, and the hon. member for Lunenburg challenged him to say with whom these contracts were made, and he made the suggestion that these contracts were made with Japanese. The hon. member for Vancouver demanded proof of that fact. I think I am in a position to give him proof. One has only got to look at the patent facts. The restrictions proposed to be made on these licenses deal only with Japanese. There are no restrictions on Indians or whites. Consequently if the cannery man made a contract with an Indian or a white a month or a year in advance, nothing would happen to them. The cannery man could not lose on these fellows because there is no restriction with regard to them as to the number of licenses to be issued. The only restrictions are as to the number to be issued to the Japanese, and it must follow that it is on contracts with Japanese that they are standing to lose. The matter is a small one and I see no reason why the hon. member should have been ashamed to tell the facts that the cannery men fear they are going to lose something on their contracts made in advance with their Japanese friends.
I know the point made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and also by the hon. member for Vancouver South. The point is in part well taken. They claim that the grievance of the cannery men is not the reduction of the Japanese licenses but the failure to carry out a pledge made by someone in the Marine and Fisheries department. I thoroughly understand that is the point to which they wish to confine the debate, but you cannot confine it to that narrow issue because the cannery men's position is clearly set forth in their telegrams and according to what they say the issue cannot be so narrowed down. If the cannery men stood to make money out of this departure from the pledge given by somebody in the Fisheries department do we suppose they would be coming here complaining? This action is taken because of the cannery men's fear that they are going to lose money, and that is why their cause is being championed here. Therefore it is entirely legitimate for us to consider, in reviewing the whole question whether they are or are not going to lose money in consequence of this alleged change of policy on the part of the Fisheries department.
There is another thing that I would like to point out. While the changes have been rung on the terms 'TO per cent" and "40 per cent" that is hardly a fair thing. That only applies to one river, and possibly two-the Skeena and the Naas-it does not apply to the other rivers. Now, the regulations suggested by the department were not that the 10 per cent should apply all over British Columbia, and it is quite unfair to use that as a comparison as against 40 per cent. It is done to create the idea that some sudden, violent, drastic change has been carried out by the department in consequence of the report of the Fisheries Commission. That is not so. The scale of reductions suggested by the departmental officials runs from 10 per cent in one case up to as high as 50 per cent in some places; and while I would not suggest that 40 per cent is the average, because it would not be so, still I wish to press the point that it is not a comparison between the 10 and 40 per cent but possibliy, on one or two cases at least, between 50 per cent and 40 per cent. The 40 per cent is probably more than the average but still there are a number of places where it was graded from 10, 15, 25, 40 and 50 per cent.
Now as to the report of the Fisheries Commission, in nearly every instance the cannery men themselves appreciated the fact that the economic situation in British Columbia was so desperate in regard to the white population that they admitted-reluctantly in most cases but they did admit-that a reduction was coming. They, of course, wanted to make the reduction as low as possible, because they think it is profitable to hire Japanese, but they did in nearly every instance, with the exception of one or two-and we heard some 197 witnesses in all-agree that a reduction was coming, so they lent themselves, at least, to some reduction. Now, the great point stressed in the letters and in the telegrams to the department, some of which were read this afternoon, was that the cannery men would be in a hole on account of this restriction; that they would not be able to get white or Indian fishermen to take the place of those restricted. That is the sum and substance of their argument. Well, I would like to ask those gentlemen who are championing their cause so ably this afternoon if they ever made any attempt to get white or Indian fishermen? It is on record-when speaking on the subject of immigration I quoted from a newspaper clipping stating the fact-that 30 or 40 Norwegian fishermen had passed through Winnipeg on their way to Prince Rupert, where the hon. member for
British Columbia Fisheries

Skeena (Mr. Stork) resides, to engage in the fisheries industry, induced, no doubt, by the expected reduction of Japanese licenses. Now, if there is likely to be any shortage of fishermen as a result of this reduction in Japanese licenses there is a source from which the canners can get men to take their places. Canners will not get very many fishermen by simply sitting in their offices and sending out telegrams.
There is another point to which I would like to draw attention. The importance of this fight, I may say, centres round the Skeena river because it is there where the department's reduction was 10 per cent and 40 per cent was recommended by the commission. We took ample evidence there. We spent a lot of time on the Skeena river which is a most important river-probably the most important river-in British Columbia now in salmon production and the evidence ran-I have not the figures at present, the debate has been brought on so suddenly-but speaking from recollection I think the united Japanese, white and Indian fishermen on that river last year would be in the neighbourhood of 1,100 or 1,080, of which 600 or 700 would be Japanese, or it may be 680. Man after man, of their own accord, swore in the witness box that the fishing would be much better on the Skeena river, if, and had been much better, when, there were only 800 boats on that river. Some of the cannery men themselves pleaded with us to go back to the old system of restricted licenses and only to put 800 boats on. They said it would be much better for the cannery men, and much better for the conservation of the fish. If a reduction of 40 per cent is made on the Skeena river it will only bring the number of fishermen down to something like the former number of 800, even if no extra whites are obtained. If the records are consulted of the number of salmon taken on the Skeena river during the last ten years it will be found that the greatest quantity was caught when the number of boats allowed was only 800. And possibly therefore the cannery men will not be ruined, possibly they will not be bankrupt, if the reduction to 40 per cent is made, because when there were 800 boats at work the fishery enured to the profit of the canneryman. I am not saying that we should not take the word of the cannery men, but if you were to ask me for my candid opinion of their telegrams, as to whether I thought they were entirely accurate, I would say, certainly not. We had evidence given last year before our Fisheries committee of the House where cannery men came and swore what the results would be if certain action were not [DOT] 
taken. One gentleman said: My cannery will not run again if you do not do so and so. I made it my business during the tour of the commission last year to inquire whether the cannery of the gentleman who had made this statement was still running and, singular to relate, I found he was still running his canneries in spite of his statement on oath that if we did not do what he wanted us to do he would close up his establishment. I do not say that the cannery men are less credible than any other body of men engaged in promoting their own interest; it is only human nature for a man who is seeking some favour from the government to exaggerate his case to the very limit.
While our interim report was not given to the department, I find, until December, the recommendation was well known in British Columbia before that.
How did it become known in British Columbia?

The information leaked out
through some official or officials. Before the commission adjourned we had agreed to keep the nrntter secret until the chairman had presented the report; but the recommendation became known in British Columbia before he got as far as Winnipeg on his way home. Now why did not the cannery men, if they were sensible business men, after hearing of our interim report, wait a little while until they found out what was going to be done? The minister has dealt with what we might refer to as the December pledge, but there is also what I may refer to as the June pledge. The hon. member for Burrard,-and to-day is the first time I heard of it, in almost the first sentence of his speech used these words: "The department in June assured the canners"-in British Columbia of course- "that irrespective of the report of the commission no change would be made." Now we did not meet until the middle or end of August and yet in June those cannery men were assured by somebody in the department that it did not matter what our report was they were perfectly safe, no change would be made. I think that is the most remarkable and the most important statement that has been made here to-day, and an investigation into that is of far greater importance, in the interests of the fishing industry of British Columbia, than the question that is more immediately before us to-day. Who sent that statement, who gave that assurance, and at whose solicitation was it done? This assurance did not come like a bolt from the blue. I submit it is reasonable to say that

the cannery men in British Columbia asked for that assurance before they got it, and if that is so then I submit that there is-what shall I say a fraternity that bodes no good to the public weal between the cannery men in British Columbia and some officials in this city or elsewhere. I do not know from whom or where the assurance came. It may have come from Ottawa or from elsewhere, but wherever it comes from, it shows there is too great an association between some of the cannery men and government officials. Long before this commission was in existence we had reason to entertain this idea, and we have had reason to entertain the opinion since. If the cannery men of British Columbia feel that they have any grievance, if they feel that they have not been dealt with fairly, they had better seek redress from those who gave them the assurance they had no business to give, which assurance no right thinking government or minister should support. In other words, let them seek redress from their friends who gave them the unjustified assurance.
There is just one other matter I wish to refer to. The Minister has commented on the difference between the attitude of some hon. members from British Columbia when we were discussing last year in a more or less academic way the subject of Asiatic exclusion, always a popular thing to spread oneself on, and to-day when it came to the practical application of those principles. But I can assure the hon. minister that there is a saving element in the members from British Columbia who are truly consistent in the matter, who neither employ nor affiliate themselves with employers of Japanese. We have nothing to do with them, and poor and weak prophets though we may be, we have not bowed the knee to Baal, nor worshipped at the shrine of the Golden Calf.

Might I ask the hon member not to discuss any matter other than the motion which is before the House. The question of the salmon fisheries in British Columbia is not at issue on this motion. It would form by itself a subject of a special substantive motion. Therefore, I would ask the hon. member not to discuss that matter.
Mr. MeQLARRIE: I will endeavour not to wander, in fact I do not think I was wandering, with all due respect. What I was arguing was this: That even if there were not as

British Columbia Fisheries
many fishermen employed, this year in the British Columbia waters, it would be a good thing for the conservation of the fish, and consequently it would be a good thing for those interested in fisheries, the cannery men as well as the others.
Something has been said as to the information which the members of the Fishery Commission had in regard to the pledges made by the department, and I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I saw in the press of British Columbia some time last winter a statement that no changes would be made during the coming year. I will not contend for a moment that I was labouring under any false impression or any misapprehension as to true conditions.
I heard that this statement had been made- at least, it was stated in the press that an arrangement of that kind had been arrived at. So that I came down to Ottawa with my eyes open. I am in the same position as the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork), and when we discussed our official report we did so with the information that some such statement had been made. But as far as these definite and concrete pledges are concerned, they were not before us.
Now on the other phase of the question, whether there will be this 40 per cent reduction or not, X must say that I stand by the report of the Fisheries Commission. I think the cut is justified, and I think credit is due to the minister for carrying out the recommendations of the Fisheries Commission. As far as I am concerned, ever since I came to this House-and I was in the last parliament-I have hammered away on this question of the number of Japanese employed in the British Columbia fisheries, and I must say that I appreciated the action of the government and of the minister in referring the question of the British Columbia fisheries to the standing committee on Marine and Fisheries, because that committee up to that time, so far as British Columbia fisheries were concerned, had been dead. I say that ^ the minister is entitled to credit for having given his permission to refer the matter of British Columbia fisheries to the standing committee. He is also entitled to credit for having agreed to the appointment of the sub-committee which went out to British Columbia, because if that sub-committee had not gone out there the fishing interests, and particularly the fishermen would not have been able to place their case before this parliament or before the committee. I feel that the minister is entitled to credit for having appointed that commission, and if he is now going to carry out its recommendations he should also be
[Mr. McQuarrie.3
given credit for that. The British Columbia Fisheries Commission gave everyone an opportunity to be heard. We went into all the different districts and gave every interest a fair chance. Some of the interests that were concerned did not avail themselves of that opportunity; they were inclined to pooh-pooh the commission altogether. Well, that is their fault, not ours, because as I have said everyone was given the fullest opportunity to be heard. Nobody was prevented from giving his evidence; and I will say for the chairman of the commission and the other members of it who are not of the same party as myself, that they carried out their duties in a conscientious manner and treated everyone fairly. So far as I can see they used their best judgment in coming to their conclusions, and I agree with them in the report that they have submitted, except in one particular which has been referred to. I do not wish for a moment to be placed in the position of backing up any misstatement or misrepresentation which has been made, but I do say that I stand by the report of the Fisheries Commission and am of the opinion that it should be carried out. We should make the 40 per cent cut this year, and I do not believe that the canners or anyone else will be harmed thereby. I am firmly-convinced that if we make this cut and stick to it, and make other reductions later on as conditions warrant, we shall get the fisheries back into the control of the white men and Indians as it should be. That would be better for British Columbia, I am sure, and better for the whole of Canada.

As one of the members who happen to have been honoured by appointment to the Fisheries Commission, I agree with a great deal of what has been said this afternoon. I do not, however, agree with the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), who endeavoured to take an unfair advantage of the fact, that he had the floor. I do not presume to be a modern Pythagoras, like the leader of the Opposition, who sets up a premise of his own devising, the fruit of his own imagination, and arrives at a conclusion altogether irrespective of whether that conclusion is justified by logic or not. So far as the forty per cent reduction in Japanese licenses is concerned, I may say that during the time the commission sat in British Columbia I was probably one of the most strenuous opponents to oriental fishermen being permitted to engage in Canadian fisheries. After hearing all the evidence, however, I concluded that I was possibly too harsh in the judgment which I had previously arrived at, and when we came

British Columbia Fisheries
to draw up our conclusions, with a view to
unanimity the reduction was placed at forty per cent, although I may remark-and I do not think it is unprofessional to do so-that there were members of the commission who wished at one fell stroke to make the reduction 100 per cent. While I did not sign a minority report I was almost compelled to come to the decision that was reached by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) that in view of the lateness of the season we were probably taking the canners unaware. The canners, however, were and are well organized and they are in a fit position to look after themselves. In the light of all the evidence that subsequently came before the commission I concluded, therefore, that I could best serve the interests of the country and of the fisheries by agreeing with the majority, who decided that- it was time to have a reduction of forty per cent.
I do not believe that I am giving away any secret of the commission when I say that the idea of the majority was not only a reduction of forty per cent but that there should be such a forty per cent reduction at the outset, and a sufficient reduction from year to year looking to the total exclusion of Asiatics from the British Columbia fisheries within a period of five years. So that I think the British Columbia canners have reason to congratulate themselves that they are not faced to-day with a recommendation calling for a one hundred per cent reduction in-stanter instead of a gradual reduction with a view to the total exclusion of Asiatics from these fisheries within five years. As the report now stands, all that the commission has recommended is a reduction of forty per cent for this year. We are now functus officio so to speak; and our duties have been discharged. Had we recommended to the minister what was in the mind of the majority of the commissioners at the time of the drafting of the interim report we should now be contemplating the total exclusion of Asiatics at once or within five years. I repeat, therefore, that those British Columbia canners who employ Asiatics should congratulate themselves on the fact that they have not to contend with the extreme of what was in the mind of the commission at the time of the making of the report.
Something has been said about what some of the departmental officials stated to the British Columbia trade during the time that the commission was functioning. I have no brief whatever for the departmental officials, but I believe that they were actuated by sincere motives. We may not all agree that the De-99
partment of Marine and Fisheries is perfectly administered; but the acme of efficiency is not to be found in any branch of the service, any more than it is to be found in any department of the business world. I believe, however, that the Department of Marine and Fisheries were actuated by the very best of motives. At the time when this letter, which has been read, was given to the people we had put in an interim report. The department had no knowledge of the time when the final report would be received. There was no definitely stated time as to when we would submit that report. True enough, if we had put the country to the expense of calling the members of the commission from British Columbia and from the Maritime provinces to meet in solemn conclave in the city of Ottawa to consider the matter and then make a report, the department would have been in a position to give definite information to the trade in British Columbia as to what they could expect for the present year. But it was not deemed advisable that the commissioners should all come together in Ottawa prior to a session of parliament. Therefore a letter was written to the British Columbia canners informing them that so far as could be foreseen nothing definite would be done for the year 1923. However, pursuant to the promise made by the right hon. the leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King), parliament met towards the close of January of this year and the commissioners had an opportunity of coming together. They considered the evidence they had received in British Columbia, together with various matters that had been presented by the canners and others from that province in the way of telegrams, letters and memoranda. However in the light of the evidence adduced and our visit to the locus in quo we came to the conclusion that it would be in the best interests of the country that a forty per cent reduction should be made this year, and we notified the minister accordingly. After a conference with his officials and taking all the circumstances into consideration, undoubtedly the minister concluded that this reduction should be carried out this season.
To my mind the canners of British Columbia have not been in any way handicapped by the action taken. A canner must estimate what his pack is going to be for the next year so that he may be in a position to buy his tin-for his containers and all his other supplies. As a result of this forty per cent reduction of licenses to Japanese fishermen he is not restrained from getting the catch that he estimated, because he has the opportunity of employing whites and Indians to make up the



British Columbia Fisheries
deficiency. Therefore the putting into effect of this forty per cent reduction will not prevent the British Columbia canner from getting his estimated amount of fish. It is interesting to observe that on the basis of the amount of fish the Japanese caught la3t year the reduction of their licenses by forty per cent will not affect the estimated amount of any canner's business by more than ten per cent and, as I have already said, he can make up this difference by employing whites and Indians, and the consequence will be no loss to the canner and the encouragement of white fishermen.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not leading the government. I have been termed a radical and everything else imaginable almost, but this I know and know full well that I am a Canadian animated with the desire to see justice done to my fellow Canadians. I do not admit that I entertain all the varied views imputed to me, but I do claim to know one or two things about the fisheries in which my forebears were engaged at the place of my birth, and from my experience as an official of the Department of Marine and Fisheries for years-I believe some weeks of which were under you, Mr. Speaker-I truly claim to know at least something about the fisheries and the administration thereof in this country. On the strength of that knowledge I say, in all fairness to my colleagues who were engaged with me in the department, in all fairness to the white fishermen of this country, and in all fairness to the excellent man who is now Minister, of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), that they have done what is right, I do not believe there is a Canadian citizen from Cape Breton to Vancouver Island who will condemn either the report of the fisheries commission or the action of the minister in putting its recommendations into effect. Therefore, before attempting to take any advantage, political or otherwise, from the report-which I believe is in the best interests of this country-any hon. member who stands up in this House and makes allegations should be seized of the facts before doing so, and not make vainglorious declamations against the action of the minister when these allegations are based upon a vivid imagination and ignorance of conditions.
My right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), who is not in his seat at the moment, took advantage of the fact that he had the floor and would not permit me to ask him a c'ertain question, for undoubtedly he showed up his pretensions and instead of giving a pertinent answer, seized the opportunity to indulge in some characteristic insinuations. If he were in his place, I would tell him that though he 
possesses the title of "right honourable," and I am simply a humble hon. member, I would be glad to meet him on any platform or in any forum to discuss the rights of the fishermen of this country.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has done right in putting into effect what the people have demanded. My hon. friends from British Columbia on both sides of the House stood in their places last year and voted for Asiatic exclusion. My colleagues and I got along most amicably together on the fisheries commission.
