To this commission I submit must be accorded the credit of having recommended to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and the hon. minister must be credited therewith, the first practical step that has ever been taken by the government of Canada to make British Columbia a white country-something which the people have been fighting for for many years. Consequently when the right hon. leader of the Opposition stands in his place and tries to appease the British Columbia canners by attacking the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries for endeavouring to make that province a white country by putting into effect practical fisheries' regulations- regulations that will not only m'ake the province a better country for the white man but a better country for good fishermen to live in, I say he is doing something which is not consistent either with the best interests of British Columbia or of the Dominion generally.	*

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Kootenay) (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am
satisfied that if my hon. friend for Burrard (Mr. Clark) and his seconder, the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Ladner) had realized where this discussion would lead them they would not have precipitated it this afternoon. Personally, and as a representative from the province of British Columbia, I rather regret the course that has been followed by them, for the simple reason that I believe it is the desire of the members from my province to show a united front in regard to orientals. However, I am not going to discuss that phase of the matter.
During the discussion some fairly thin ice has been crossed. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) stated that if the fisheries commission which was appointed to examine into the question under discussion, and who made a careful and exhaustive study of conditions last summer in the various ports of British Columbia, had known that these instructions had gone out in December from the Fisheries department they would not have

British Columbia Fisheries
brought in the recommendations which they later rendered. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie), a member of that commission, stated that it was only known to him through the press or through channels of gossip or conversation that such instructions had gone out. Now, Sir, in order that there may be no misunderstanding in the minds of hon. members in regard to the knowledge that the commissioners had, I would read a short letter dated December 23rd, 1922. It is as follows:
Dear Mr. McQuarrie,-In view of the fact that the final report of the British Columbia Fisheries Commission, of which you are a member, will not be submitted until after the House meets, and as it is embarrassing to the whole industry to have frequent changes in the regulations and policy governing it, it has been deemed best to await the final report of the commission before reaching decisions on the recommendations contained in the interim report.
Hence those engaging in the industry have been advised that no action will be taken on the report that will affect the season of 1923. This does not involve that there will be no reduction in the number of fishery licenses that will be available to naturalized orientals. The reduction of such licenses that was decided upon last June, before the appointment of the commission, will be effective so far as next year is concerned.
This letter signed by the Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bureau) was sent to each and every member of the commission, so the commissioners in drawing their final report had knowledge of the action of the department at that date.
Now, what did the commissioners do in the face of that knowledge? In their final report to the minister they say:
The representations that have been made by the various interests concerned in the British Columbia fisheries, as well as the objections raised by certain officials of the department since the publication of the commission's interim report have been carefully considered by the commissioners before the writing of their final report. Our conclusions and recommendations as hereinafter set forth have therefore been reached and agreed upon in the full light of the said further representations.
So we have this position-and it has not been fairly represented to-day-that the commission which spent last summer investigating this problem in order that we might reach proper conclusions upon it, the fishing interests, were advised that the regulations would continue with the reduction as proposed last June, over 1923, and the commission, in the face of that, recommended to the minister that their report, involving a forty per cent reduction, should be carried out. That change in policy took place in February of this year, some three or four months before the opening of the fishing season. I do not believe there is sound ground for the complaint that is made here to-day. I do not believe this is
99J
an urgent matter or one that requires such a debate as we have had here this afternoon

Mr. Speaker, I think it must be apparent to the House that the minister has made no satisfactory explanation of his course in blowing hot and cold in this matter. No sufficient reason has been given for breaking what to all intents and purposes was understood by the canners of British Columbia as a pledge. The government's action was not businesslike; it was unfair to the canners. My conclusion is that the minister, or his department, for which he must take responsibility, was too hasty in sending out that first telegram, for which there was no necessity; too hasty in making that pledge by wire. A promise, or what can fairly be considered as a promise, was made; it could not be kept- at any rate, the government determined that it should not be kept, with the consequence that somebody has been injured. Well, that often happens, and the government must take the consequences and pay the damages if there are damages. For myself I have not much sympathy with people who make losses through the employment of orientals. I think it is better to let them take the consequences; they will probably be less likely to employ orientals in the future and will have less to do with them. I do think that the canners might very well have been put on their guard by the wording of that telegram, which was to the effect that irrespective of the findings of the commission there would be no changes in the regulations. That should have been a warning to them that the report of the commission might have the effect of bringing about a change in the regulations. It is true that the action of the minister brings about a result that is most desirable I say, to the great majority of the people of British Columbia, namely, a reduction of the employment of orientals in the industry in that province, and I am sure that no one would be more pleased with that result than the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner). No one would be better pleased with that result than they, and I am sure they can congratulate themselves on the effort made by them at the last session, and particularly by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) in impressing upon this House and the government the need for action to curb oriental immigration into British Columbia. They can, I say, very well congratulate themselves upon the fact that their efforts have met with some success. But on the other hand I think that the minister

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
should acknowledge the mistake-that is, the mistake of the department-and not attemj.it to take refuge behind the popularity of the anti-oriental movement with the idea of covering up his mistake, because that quite evidently is the object of the attempt put forth by him and his supporters here to-day. But, as the right hon. leader of the Opposition, (Mr. Meighen) has said, no member is so dull ns to be misled by this old device of drawing a herring across the trail; even though we are talking about fish, no one is to be diverted by that from the point raised by this resolution. The point is that what the canners understood as a pledge was given by the minister, and for reasons which are perhaps well grounded he has seen fit not to carry out that pledge but has rather made a much more material reduction in the number of Japanese licenses. That is the point under discussion in connection with this resolution, not the question whether Japanese licenses should be reduced or abolished. For my part I support any administration that takes action to meet the oriental menace, which is in fact a real one. But as I say, no one should be misled by the putting forward of the anti-oriental question with the view of covering up the mistake made by the government in this instance.

As I pointed out a moment ago, I propose first to deal with what was known as the Canadian National railway system prior to October last.
General Conditions throughout 1922
Before dealing with the income account, Canadian National Railways, a word or two concerning conditions and circumstances affecting 1922 operations might not be amiss. The gross earnings for 1922 decreased by $6,866.509.93. Freight, passenger and express earnings were all less than in 1921. The decrease in passenger traffic is a disappointment in view of the improved quality of service provided, and also in view of the fact that the rate for passenger travel in Canada is, generally speaking, slightly below the prevailing rates in the United States. A good year was expected, and provided for, but the traffic did not materialize.
While the tonnage of freight carried was slightly higher, and the average haul and train loading improved, the freight earnings fell off to the extent of $3,901,611.86, and the average rate per ton per mile-ton-mile rate -fell from 1.041 cents in 1921 to .889 cent in 1922, a decrease of 14.6 per cent.
It so happened that the improvement in traffic was largely confined to the final half of the year when reduced rates were in effect.
I am offering no opinion as to whether the improvement in traffic was due to the reduction in rates or to a good crop and consequent general improvement in business, but this much can be said: that on account of its widespread mileage in the nine provinces, the traffic movement of the Canadian National Railways is a reliable indication of the state of trade in the country as a whole.
System car loading improved in the early months of the year, and appreciably so from towards the end of April, when, until the crop commenced to move, a daily loading of from two to three hundred cars more than the previous year was maintained. During the crop movement the improvement averaged a thousand cars a day. The all-rail movement of grain, which commenced in October, three months earlier than usual, contributed to the density of freight traffic on eastern lines. It is estimated that the restoration of the Crows-nest rates on grain reduced the earnings during the last half of the year by six and a half million dollars. Notwithstanding this reduction in rates, the earnings exceeded the operating expenses in September, October and November. In each of the other nine months there was an adverse balance, the smallest deficit occurring in May and the heaviest in January, February and December.
In making the statement that the restoration of the Crowsnest pass rates reduced the earnings during the last half of the year by six and a half million dollars, that estimate, of course, is based on the assumption that had the old rates remained the traffic would have been as heavy.
Income Account
The gross operating revenue for the year was $120,135,956.71, as against $127,002,466.64 in 1921; the operating expenses $129,872,274.75 as against $143,222,802.55; leaving a net deficit from railway operation of $9,736,318.04, as compared with $16,220,335.91 for the previous year.
The addition of tax accruals-which by way, are not classed by railway accountants as real operating expenses-brings the total operating deficit for 1922 up to $11,085,081.33 as against $17,805,365.16 for 1921. Non-operat-

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
ing income-car rentals, rental of joint facilities, express, mails, elevators, etc.- amounting this year to 85,644,217.22, is offset by the usual deductions from gross income-hire of equipment, joint facilities, etc.-amounting to $4,421,180.49, leaving the total deficit before fixed charges $9,862,044.60, as compared with $16,212,063.22 in 1921.
The fixed charges amounted, in 1922, to $41,241,252.31, of which $32,711,546.22 pertain to the Canadian Northern, and $8,529,706.09 to the Grand Trunk Pacific. These fixed charges swell the total Canadian National deficit to $51,103,296.91 as compared with $56,989,978.82 in 1921.
In the statement which will be placed on Hansard, it will be seen that the 1921 figures do not entirely agree with the figures brought down a year ago. At that time, the operating results of the St. John and Quebec Railway were separately shown. As the St. John and Quebec results have been included in 1922 totals it was necessary to add in the 1921 results to make the figures comparable.
Analysis of Net Operating Deficit.
The net operating deficit was $9,736,318.04, compared with $16,220,335.91 in 1921. The net operating deficit of the Canadian Government Railways is $2,496,721.91 as against $5,714,732.90 in 1921. Of this, the Intercolonial and branch lines were reponsible for $2,302,703.36, compared with $4,457,035.75 in 1921; the Prince Edward Island District, $634,588.66 as against $617,158.93 the previous year; the Transcontinental-lines east of Armstrong- $875,233.02 as against $1,964,730.23 in 1921; Transcontinental lines-west of Armstrong and east of Winnipeg, including the Grand Trunk Pacific Lake Superior Branch-an operating surplus of $1,488,833, as against an operating surplus of $1,523,547.90 in 1921; the St. John and Quebec Railway, a deficit of $148,078.67 compared with $127,434.15 the previous year; Hudson Bay railway, $24,951.43 as against $71,921.08 in 1921. I must explain, in reference to the Hudson Bay railway, that the figures are not comparable, as the periods in the two years were not the same. A closer analysis of the figures, using the same periods, will show that the operating deficit of the Hudson Bay railway in 1921 was not $71,921 but rather about $50,000.
The Canadian Northern operating deficit was reduced from $6,475,911.14 in 1921 to $2,946,729.72 in 1922, but the operating deficit of the Grand Trunk Pacific increased from $4,029,691.87 to $4,292,866.41 during the same period.

Decreased Operating Expenses
I will now refer to the decreased operating expenses. I think I might interject that an analysis of the statement will show that the marked improvement for the year' 1922 is the result of a large decrease in the cost of operating. If hon. gentlemen have followed me closely they will have seen that the first few statements made concerning the traffic were a little pessimistic on account of decrease in earnings; but the present statement is by no means pessimistic because the management was able to reduce the expenses of operation by a greater ratio than characterized the reduction of traffic. Operating expenses decreased $13,350,527.96, and the results for the year show that the expenditures were well controlled, there being reductions in the .cost both of maintenance and of transportation. The management assure me that the condition of the physical properties was improved during the year notwithstanding that maintenance of way expenses were reduced by $2,656,340.92, and maintenance of equipment expenses by $1,225,612.86. As already pointed out, more business was moved, though $11,299,471.65 less in transportation expenses was spent to move same, in addition to the maintenance savings.
Slight reductions in pay for certain classes of employees, a decrease in the average number of employees-to be later referred to- and reduced cost of materials contributed to the improved showing, but the management feel that in the main credit should be given to greater efficiency of freight traffic, handling more, miles per car per day and a small increase in load per car mile. The cost of yard operation was also considerably reduced, measured on the basis of the number of cars handled.
Operating Ratio
What is meant by the "operating ratio" is how much money it takes to earn a dollar. Shortly, I may say that when it takes $1.05 to earn $1 there is a deficit; when the earning expenditure is one dollar or less there is no deficit. The operating ratio for the year was 108.10, as compared with 112.77 in 1921 and 129.32 in 1920. The operating ratios of the component parts of the National System were as follows:

Traffic Results-Steam Lines
The National lines carried 11,331,226 passengers during 1922, or 606,923 less than in 1921. the average haul per passenger was 60.84 miles, compared with 59.87 miles in the previous year, and the passenger earnings were $17,919,602.17, a decrease of $2,289,218.02 compared with 1921.
The system handled 22,426,403 tons of revenue freight, an increase of 1,164,803 tons. The average haul also increased from 423.19 miles to 449.97 miles, but the freight revenue, which was $89,726,925.51, fell off $3,901,611.86 because of lower rates.
The average earnings per traffic train mile were $3.52 which was 8 cents less than in 1921, and the operating expenses $3.82, which was 25 cents less than the previous year. The average operating revenue per mile of road was $6,885.33, which was $438.16 less than in 1921, and the average operating expense per mile of road was $7,466.23, a decrease of, $817.30. The average load per freight train increased from 482.66 tons to 548.34 tons.
Analysis of Operating Expenses
Out of each dollar spent by the National Railways on operating account during 1922, the following expenditures were made: 24.13 cents for maintenance of way and structures; 23.53 cents for maintenance of equipment; 2.23 cents for traffic expenses-soliciting, etc, -46.57 cents for rail line transportation-en-ginemen, trainmen, yardmen, station employees, etc.-1.42 cents for miscellaneous operations-dining and buffet, hotels restaurants, etc.-2.79 cents for general expenses- general offices, clerical and legal staff, etc.- and 0.67 for transportation for investment- i.e., the movement of materials entering into the property. This split of the expenditure dollar closely approximates the figures for 1921, except transportation costs, which are 3.61 cents less.

subtopic: ANNUAL STATEMENT BY THE ACTING MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
At six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was analyzing the operating costs. Now I shall take up the item of labour.
Labour
Out of gross earnings of $120,135,956.71, the management paid out $82,390,245.42 in wages, including betterments, about six and a half million dollars less than the 1921 total pay-roll. Operating labour cost $72,969,378.48, or almost 10 millions less than the previous year. The ratio of operating labour costs to gross earnings was 60.74 for the system, as against 65-02 in 1921, an improvement of 4-28 per cent. The average number of employees in 1922 was 58,398 compared with 60,315 in 1921, a decrease of almost two thousand.
During the first four months of the year, labour forces were lighter than in the corresponding period in the preceding year. In May, June and July maintenance forces were increased with the general object of having track and other conditions improved for the fall movement, which gave every indication of being heavy. From August to December, inclusive, substantially the same force was maintained as in 1921, although more tonnage was moved.
Locomotive Coal Purchases
Locomotive coal to the extent of 3,053,829 tons was purchased during 1922 at an average price of $5.47 and a total cost of $16,711,35522. Of this 2,198,039 tons was Canadian coal, at an average price of $4.83, or $10,621,037.57; 798,330 tons American coal, at an average price of $7.13, or $5,693,783.90 and 57,460 British coal at an average price of $6.90, or $396,533.75 In 1921 the average price of Canadian coal was $5.71 and of the American coal $6.47. During that year 2,505,389 tons of Canadian coal were purchased and 977,696 tons of American. Less coal to the extent of 429,256 tons was purchased during 1922.
Equipment
A statement showing details of equipment on hand, retirements and deliveries during the year, will be included with those to be handed ini Briefly it shows that the Canadian National system had 1951 locomotives and 87,482 cars on December 31, 1922, as against 1,973 locomotives and 88,478 cars on December 31, 1921. Also, for the information of the House, I shall put in a statement of new equipment ordered during the current year, totalling $20,250,600.85. The statement will show the number and type of equipment, the name of the builder, and the price. Unfortunately prices are still very high. For mountain type locomotives we are paying 74,500 and for the Mikado type $66,500. First-class coaches still cost $35,443,

C.N!R.-Minister's Statement
as against $16,586 in 1914., and standard sleepers $49,400, compared with $28,250 in 1915; mail cars, which could be built for $11,500 before the war, now cost $29,650; express refrigerator cars, which cost $4,642 in 1918, now cost $10,550; steel baggage cars, which cost $6,666 in 1915, cost $24,750 now; general service freight cars which cost $1,346 in 1914 and $3,250 in 1920, are now priced at $2,950; box cars which could be bought for $1,150 in 1914 and were $2,950 in 1920, are now $2,555. It is only fair to explain that car equipment purchased from 1914 to 1917, inclusive, was fitted with wooden and steel sills, and from 1918 to 1923 with steel sills and steel framing, and was also of greater capacity.
Betterments
The betterments effected during the year included the laying of 444 miles of new 85 lb. rail and 172 miles of second-hand relay rails, principally on western lines; the putting in of 5,910,014 ties and 1,030 miles of ballast; 50 new water supplies and 11 new water tanks; 432 miles of fencing and 315 sidings and siding extensions; 41 new stations and 16 station extensions; 9 new freight sheds and 9 freight-shed extensions; 64 bunkhouses and section houses; 77 other buildings, 15 coaling plants, 406 culverts, 32 bridges and 163 bridges and trestles filled. A statement of the larger betterment items will, as usual, be handed in to Hansard.
New Construction During 1922
With the exception of the Long Lac cut off no new construction was undertaken during the year, and on the cut off only preparatory work was done up to December 31 last. The late minister pointed out a year ago that in the West 'alone construction had been projected which would entail an expenditure of $25,000,000 to bring to completion, but in view of financial conditions and the impending reorganization of the National Railway Board and management, the betterment programme for 1922 would consist of finishing work in hand as far as track had been laid, leaving the new board free to advise as to further extensions. In accordance with the policy indicated, no new grading or tracklaying was undertaken during the year under review, though considerable ballasting and surfacing was completed and necessary buildings and structures erected. Details of this will be supplied, also as to the 172.3 miles of new lines in the West turned over to the operating department for permanent operation. This mileage was under operation on behalf of the construction department, with restrictions as
TMr. Graham.]
to speed, at the beginning of 1922 and was merely brought to completion during the year.
So far, Mr. Speaker, I have dealt only with the railway system known up to October last year as the Canadian National, not with that portion of it formerly known as the Grand Trunk.

Now let me take up the Grand Trunk. To one who, like myself, has lived along the old Grand Trunk nearly all his lifetime the passing of this road from its original status even to become part of our national system is somewhat of a tragedy. We who have known the Grand Trunk so well since our boyhood almost reverence the old line. Of course, now that it has become part of our national system of railways I think I may be allowed to express the view that, given a fair opportunity, it will prove a splendid asset to the Dominion.
The Grand Trunk experienced in a general way the same difficulties as the Canadian National, though it did not come within the

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
influence of the Crowsnest reduction. It carried fewer passengers, with consequent loss in revenue, and while freight tonnage and freight earnings increased somewhat, the average revenue per ton per mile was 4 per cent less than the previous year. This was stated to be owing to the reductions in Canadian freight rates effective December 1st, 1921, and August 1st, 1922; also to reductions in United States and International freight rates effective January 1st and July 1st, 1922. The system carried 940,000 fewer tons of coal and coke for reasons which are well known; but loss tonnage was more than offset by increases in general commodities, the most prominent of which were lumber* and forest products, including wood pulp, building materials, motor cars, flour and iron and steel products. The decrease of $1,668,459.55 in passenger revenue, while contributed to by 1,124,181 fewer passengers, was in part due to a reduction in International fares at the beginning of the year. There was also a slight falling off in express earnings.

This is a fairly complete statement, I submit, of what has taken place during the year 1922, and I think that under the conditions existing in the Dominion of Canada, and

C.N.B.-Minister's Statement
which exist elsewhere, perhaps all over the world, in a more aggravated degree, the better showing of our Canadian National lines at the end of 1922 is very encouraging to the people of Canada who believe that eventually a public-owned railway can be made a success in this country. The problem is not easy to work out, but if we give it a fair show I think it will work itself out. Notwithstanding the reduction in rates from the West owing to the restoration of the Crowsnest pass agreement, which represents a reduction of over six million dollars, the improvement shown is very encouraging, and when amalgamation is fully completed and traffic is carried by the lines that can carry it most advantageously, when the operation of the two great systems becomes dovetailed and friction ceases, it is reasonable to suppose that there will be a betterment in conditions.
May I interject another word? Notwithstanding the fact that psychologically some of us seem to be hard up, the improved condition of this great highway that carries the people's products reflects, I think, the improved condition of the people generally throughout the Dominion of Canada, because * it is a generally conceded fact that the condition in which the transportation companies of a country find themselves is a reflection of the condition in which the people of that country find themselves.

Now, as to next year you have all heard, no doubt, the story that our late lamented friend, Mahlon Cowan, once a brilliant member of this House, told us. In one of his election campaigns he went to see a coloured gentleman to whom he had been very kind and asked him for his support-as is usual, they tell me, when candidates are canvassing. His friend was a little reluctant to make him any pledge and he said to him "You remember, don't you Sam, that a week ago I got out of bed and went down and got you out of gaol?" "Oh, yes, I remember that." "Well, can't you give me your support after all that?" "Well, I will tell you. 'Liza and I have been talkin it over, and it's not what you have done but it is what, you is goin' to do that is goin' to influence us." In making an estimate for next year, of course, we are going to base that estimate on the view that conditions in Canada are likely to continue to improve, and while that is not unduly optimistic I think it is on the safe side.

I asked the president of the Canadian National Railways to give me a synopsis of what had been accomplished in the matter of reorganization, and he has furnished me with the following statement:
The present management took charge of the property about December first, 1922, at a session of the year

C.X.R.-Minister's Statement
when inspections, examinations and progress were difficult on account of winter conditions.
Obviously, the first effort of the management was to make as complete an inspection of the property as weather conditions would permit, in as short a time as possible, and to become acquainted with the officers and employees on the various constituent parts of the National Railway system. In addition to this, traffic conditions and problems had to be examined, as all of these were essential factors in the determination of the organization which would be necessary to operate the consolidated system.
There were three primary problems which demanded immediate attention:
1.	The determination of the kind of an organization which was to be employed in the administration of the property.
2.	The determination of the regions into which the property was to be divided for operating purposes, and the location of regional and general headquarters.
3.	The selection of officers for the various posts involved in the organization.
The study and successful solution of these three questions naturally involved examination of the property itself; the country, its productivity; the movement of traffic and the rates charged thereon; the principal lines of future commercial and agricultural development ; coupled with a general study of the economic condition of the Dominion. Perhaps the most important and difficult problem was to assess the value of officers for prospective posts, with a view to getting the right man in the right place.
The organization which has been decided upon is what may be called a strengthened divisional organization as distinguished from a departmental organization. The executive officers consist of a chairman and president, assisted by five vice-presidents as under:
1.	Vice-president in charge of operation, maintenance and construction.
2.	Vice-president in charge of financial affairs.-
3.	Vice-president in charge of insurance, immigration, development, lands, express and telegraphs.
4.	Vice-president in charge of legal affairs.
5.	Vice-president in charge of traffic.
The above executive officers represent the minimum with which, in my judgment, it would be possible to operate such a property as the Canadian National Railways; indeed, as time goes on and traffic increases, it will probably be necessary to add another vicepresident. The list above given, however, represents a considerable economy as compared with the executive officers of the old national system and the Grand Trunk Railway. Those properties had in the aggregate one chairman, two presidents, and eleven vice-presidents, with a complete staff of officers for each. There is now one chairman and president, and five vice-presidents. The actual saving in salaries of vice-presidents and their immediate office forces should be at least $150,000 a year.
It is not possible at the moment to say exactly what the total savings in the salary list will be, as the organization has been barely completed and the officers have hardly fettled into their places, and consequently the exact number of clerks and subordinates in each department has not been finally fixed; but one would be quite safe in saying that a material saving will be accomplished, and a much more efficient administrative machine provided. Most of the announcements made with respect to officers represent either a rearrangement of duties and responsibilities or the confirmation of positions which already existed. In only one or two cases have entirely new positions been created; and the net result will undoubtedly be the employment of a smaller administrative class.
The railway has been divided into three regions for operating purposes, and this feature has been so exhaustively discussed before that comment is now unnecessary. Suffice it to say that the principle followed was to give to each operating region as much autonomy and local control in the actual operation of the property as was consistent with efficient principles of administration. Every effort will be made to confine the functions of the vice-presidents and the executive officers to policies, leaving to general managers, general superintendents and superintendents the responsibility of carrying out details. In the administration of such a large property as is represented by the Canadian National Railways no other theory of organization can be successful.
Various aspects of the operation of the national system are being studied with a view to reducing expenses as rapidly as possible. For example, it has been found that the railway could advantageously do its own insuring, and this has been decided upon. It is anticipated that from this item alone there will be a saving which will approximate half a million dollars a year.
It is the intention of the present administration to apply itself as diligently as possible to the creation of new traffics and the movement of those traffics and existing traffics with a constantly increasing economy. A system of statistics is under development which will, it is hoped, enable the maximum of use to be made of engine power. An examination of timekeeping methods is under way. in order to ensure that every employee is paid all that is coming to him, but no more. New methods of storekeeping, and the custody of materials, are being developed, in order that purchases may be reduced to a minimum; and in various ways the organization is preparing to bring each department and function of the railway to as high a degree of efficiency as modem scientific knowledge will permit.
In the organization of such a property, where we employ about one hundred thousand people, scattered over nearly 23,000 miles of line, the process of consolidating and harmonizing the various forces is one which will necessarily take some time. It is, therefore, earnestly hoped that those who administer the affairs of the nation will be sufficiently patient to give those who are sincerely, honestly and conscientiously working at this problem an opportunity to show what can be accomplished before criticisms are made.
That is a statement by the president, Sir, Henry Thornton.

Then I take up the matter of insurance. The Canadian National Railways, with the full approval, I think, of the government, has decided to carry its own insurance. I might add that their Canadian Government Merchant Marine will be in the same class. The insurance on these two great. properties will amount roughly speaking, to $400,000,000. That is a good insurance business in itself. I would be delighted to be president of an insurance company that would net me approximately $400,000,000 worth of business, with the gilt-edged premium handed me every year. I would not need to do anything else or to get any more business. My renewals would keep me the rest of my time quite comfortably, and I would be able to leave something for my family. If an insurance company can do that, we believe the Canadian National Railway, with the government behind it-because we, the people, are the shareholders-can

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
carry its own insurance and make quite a saving. The insurance will not be let run wild or the risks go unprovided for. Each year when the premiums would naturally fall due, the amount of these premiums would be placed in a reserve fund for insurance purposes. Already I think the Grand Trunk has an insurance fund accumulation and I believe I am safe in saying that we have, in the several railway fire insurance funds, a rest fund of 12,000,000 with which we start. A good many policies come due on the 31st March, and in two or three weeks from now we will have substantially increased that reserve fund. Some figures have been given me which I
9 p.m. will give to the House, to be sure that I am accurate in my reference to them. But let me say that at first blush it might seem to be quite a radical policy. Well, radical policies are all right, unless they are too radical, but if during the last ten years these roads-I am speaking only of the railroads-had insured themselves, they would have saved 87,000,000 and replaced all the destroyed property. When I had the honour of being Minister of Railways in Sir Wilfrid's government, the government of course carried its own insurance. At my suggestion we established an insurance fund, not large, of course, but each year we put aside a certain amount for insurance purposes, and that fund paid all the fire losses, and had quite a substantial surplus at the end of three or four years' time.
I would like to amplify the president's reference to the change in insurance methods. The only railway property on which insurance has not been carried either by the underwriters or by means of railway insurance funds is that comprising the original group of Canadian Government Railways where the risk, about 50 millions, has been carried by the government. On the other railways, the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk groups, the insurance carried has totalled $279,425,999 and on the marine-railway as well as Canadian Government Merchant Marine-$47,620,562, a grand total of $327,046,561, on which the total annual premium or fund contribution has been $2,637,800. Had the government lines been insured-that is the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Prince Edward Island railway-the premiums or fund contributions would have totalled $2,837,800. The total losses during 1922 amounted to $1,144,279, or forty per cent of that amount. Thus, on the basis of complete insurance, the premiums would have exceeded last year's losses by $1,693,521.

The insurance records have been examined for 10 years back, and they show that our average losses over that period have been a little under seventy per cent, so that over a ten year period the saving, under the method proposed, would have been thirty per cent. Should that record be maintained, the management have every reason to expect a saving of between $750,000 and $1,000,000 a year.
In this connection I might be permitted to say that hon. members will notice on the order paper a resolution indicative of legislation to be asked in order to cover certain points in reference to the insurance. As to mortgages, we all understand that if we have a mortgage on our house we have to keep the house insured, in order to protect the individual or the company which advances the money. This is particularly the case with the rolling stock, the buildings, etc., on the railway lines. Where these have been mortgaged, they have been mortgaged under the pledge that certain insurance would be carried on the property, in order to protect the lender. In this legislation which I referred to a moment ago, all we are asked to do is that, in lieu of this insurance in a company which is supposed to have a full guarantee of stability behind it, the government will step in and guarantee that the insurance will be paid in case of the destruction of the property. In other words, the government, in regard to these loans or these mortgages held on the property, takes the place of the company and that will be perfectly satisfactory to the lenders or to the holders of security.
Hon. members will want to know now, what about constructing branch railways. Well, the completion of branch lines already started, as well as the construction of others, has been held up by the war and by financial stringency since the war. Nothing will be found in the estimates for new construction during the coming year, but I might say, in palliation of that offence, that it is the intention of the government to submit to the House a little later on, in the way of legislation, a programme for construction extending over a term of years. That will be decided by parliament after discussion, and the public will know just what the government proposes to try to do, aided by parliament, during the next three years, in the way of construction. It will not mean that parliament will be tied down to that programme of construction, but .it will be a guarantee to the public of what parliament intends to do along that line. That legislation will be brought down in due course after consideration. I know that it

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
will have the sympathy and the full consideration of the House. I might say, in that connection, that there is on the statute books at the present time what is called the Branch Lines Act-I do not know whether that is the proper title-under which not a few branch lines have been taken over by the federal government. While I believe we must be economical and keep as close in our expenditure as possible; nevertheless, we cannot blind our eyes to the other side of the picture. If the members of this parliament on both sides of the House, including the government, do not take somewhat of an optimistic view of the future of Canada, then we cannot expect the people of Canada, or the people of any other country, to believe in Canada.
While, I say, we must be as economical as possible, still there is a point beyond which economy becomes extravagance; and I believe that the programme which we hope to bring down will appeal to the members of the House. I believe it will be seen that it is not for the purpose of making extravagant expenditures but of carrying out the ideas expressed so often in this House in regard to making the people of this country more contented; for I admit that a contented settler is the best advertisement that any country can have.
As I say, we have the Branch Lines Act. Now, it may be necessary, as it has been in years past, to build short lines that will not pay. I am not prophesying, but I say that we may have to build lines that will not be profitable. And that is where a government differs somewhat from the private company. The government finds its own people have moved into a new district; or perhaps in an older part of the country they may find a railway aided by both governments and by the municipality but not properly operated. The railway itself is properly constructed, but the company has perhaps been taking everything out and putting nothing in, so that the road might just as well not be operated at all in some instances. I leave it to the consideration of the House whether, under these circumstances, it is not the duty of the government to go to the aid of people in some cases even if we know that the undertaking will not pay in dollars and cents just at the present time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I realize that it has been a long and dreary task for hon. members to listen to the statement I have submitted. The figures I have given this afternoon and evening are merely a synopsis of tabulated information which should be immediately made available in complete form for the members of the House. I would therefore request the permission of the House to hand to Hansard a copy of certain statements which it is impossible to read in full and which cannot appear unless taken as read. So that the whole situation concerning the Canadian National Railways will be before hon. members in Hansard for their consideration, and they can compare the explanations I have given with the detailed statements which they will find therein.

Canadian Government Railways. (Eastern Lines)
At Elmsdale a new 40,000 gal. steel tank was erected to replace the old wooden tank.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM (INCLUDING CENTRAL VERMONT RAILWAY)
GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM (INCLUDING CENTRAL VERMONT RAILWAY)
speechtext: If you take in the Central Vermont, a little over $4,000,000.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM (INCLUDING CENTRAL VERMONT RAILWAY)
speechtext:
Yes, if the Central Vermont is taken in the net operating surplus is a little over $4,000,000 This is the first operating surplus that parliament has had reported to it since we came out of the valley of doubt and difficulty through which we had been

C.N.B.-Minister's Statement
struggling for many years in the solution of our railway problem.
Now, while we have an operating surplus on the two roads together of some $4,000,000, we must not forget that the fixed charges which we have to pay on the systems aggregate a vastly larger sum than this. The fixed charges on the Canadian National aggregate, if I have put the figures together correctly, approximately $42,000,000. What the fixed charges are on the Grand Trunk I was not able to glean, but from my recollection of the subject I think they were some $8,000,000- that is to say, the interest on the debenture stock and the interest on the guaranteed stock which we have assumed. As a consequence, on the Canadian National Railway, where there is a deficit in operation of $9,000,000 and where we have some $42,000,000 of fixed charges to pay, we find ourselves confronted with an aggregate deficit of some $51,000,000. That $51,000,000 compares with the parallel figure for 1921 of $56,000,000 odd and with the parallel figure for 1920 of $67,000,000 odd. So it will be seen that notwithstanding the annual mounting of the fixed charges due to the fact that each year the interest on the previous deficit must be added, the improvement in operation is such that the annual deficit is year by year reduced-reduced, in millions, from 67 to 56 and then from 56 to 51 for the year through which we have just passed. These figures apply, of course, to the Canadian National Railway alone. Coming to the Grand Trunk, the profit on operation is some $12,000,000. If my figures are right as to the fixed charges-the interest on the bonded indebtedness, if you so describe it, of the system-there would be a surplus there of some $4,000,000. I am not quite sure that my figures are precisely right-though I think they are-as regards the Grand Trunk; as regards the Canadian National they are undoubtedly right.
I wish to call the attention of the House to the significance of these figures and as well to impress upon the House really what is meant by these recurring deficits in order that all will understand-though I do not wish to intimate that all do not now-just what these deficits imply, and will not think that they imply more than they do. I am not unaware-indeed, if there is anyone in this country wholly and vitally and keenly aware, it is myself-that there are influences at work-and I do not refer to railway systems- to make the people or some sections of the people believe that these deficits mean something that they do not mean at all; that they have been brought upon us because of the folly of weak-kneed, blind and stupid politicians in bringing this country into the owner-
ship of the national lines we have to-day. Of this $51,000,000-let us think of that for the time being; for by means of it the point I make can be well made clear-of this amount of deficit this year on the Canadian National, about $33,000,000 is money owed the government of Canada. That is to say, it is not money that must be found in order to let the railways stand up and proceed and give service. About $33,000,000, then, is money owed the government of Canada, and the proportion that is owed us of the total deficit is growing year by year. Because it is owed us, of course, it is a debt all the same, and I am not by any means suggest ing that it should be left out of account But we must understand that it is monej owed this country because of guarantees we gave and loans we made in years gone by, because of indebtedness we have assumed as respects the system, in regard to all of which we have our charge against the system.
What I impress at the moment is this: That assuming we go ahead, as certainly we should-and we should go ahead with accelerated speed from this on, now that we are loosened from the London management and have only one system instead of two-assuming we go ahead as we have been going for these three years, and reach the point where deficits cease, then we must remember that all these deficits of years gone by have been no loss to the people. Quite the contrary; when we get to the point where deficits cease and we commence an era of returns over fixed charges, at that point all the deficits of these previous years become interest bearing assets. Because they are in the form of loans they now add to the fixed charges year b3' year; when we overtake the fixed charges so increased from year to year and get to earning money over and above them, at that point we have gathered up all the deficits of the years that have gone and they have become assets, loans, securities, in the treasury of the Dominion, bearing interest to the people of this country. It is a common feeling-I have met many who hold this view, and I can scarcely find fault with anyone reading some of the newspapers of Canada for doing so-that after we get past the era of these terrible deficits and reach the point where operation produces -a revenue over fixed charges, then we shall have to look back and think of the money we have thrown away because of the folly of politicians; we shall have to sit in sackcloth and ashes and repent for the $50,000,000 in 1922, the $56,000,000 in 1921, the $67,000,000 in 1920, all of which is gone forever. The very contrary, let me repeat, will be the fact. When that time

C.N.R.-Mmister's Statement
comes-and it should not be long; the pace at which we reach it should henceforth be accelerated; we have been progressing towards it satisfactorily in these late years during which members of this House have listened to the returns-when that time comes all these deficits will take the form of mortgages in the treasury, bearing interest to the Canadian people.
There is another point I want to impress on the House as respects the deficits. Keeping in mind still the $51,000,000 which in 1922 is our deficit in connection with the Canadian National Railways, $33,000,000 of which is owed to the people of Canada, does anybody imagine that if any other policy had been followed, this country would have escaped those deficits? I was glad to hear from the minister an expression of confidence that, given a chance, as they have been given, and sis the results show they have been given ever since they came under the operation of the Hanna directorate, ever since they became the National Railways-continuing to give them that chance, there is abundant hope; there is, indeed, serene and well founded confidence, that good results, all that has been hoped for, will come.
I was glad to hear him say that, although I could not help but note that it was not received with any sign of applause by hon. ' gentlemen around him-hon. gentlemen who felt that applause over a statement of that sort would scarcely be in accord with their assertions and predictions of just a few years ago. Nevertheless the statement will be received with approval by the people of this country and will be received, as well, as the expression of the honest belief of the minister, who, having reviewed the history of this question and having investigated the financial situation as regards these roads, comes to the House and says this is his profound conviction.
No, we would not have escaped these deficits if any other course had been taken. As a matter of fact, it is my belief we would have had to face one of two alternatives. We would have to have faced either an utterly demoralized service given to the people of Canada by the roads, or vastly greater sums to be provided by the parliament of Canada to hold the roads in private hands. Why is such the case? The Transcontinental Railway would have had to have been run by the Grand Trunk Pacific. It would have got from the west the traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and no other traffic. The Grand Trunk Pacific would have had to have been held on its feet by the bounty of this parliament in loans of millions year after year,
operated as an isolated and almost trafficless road. The Grand Trunk would have continued to have been operated from London, under Sir Alfred Smithers and his board of directors sitting in an attic in the middle of that city, operated by Mr. Kelley here in Canada, with Mr. Kelley's methods and Mr. Kelley's directorate, and the Grand Trunk, which was at the end of its tether by the admission of its directorate in 1918, would have been out of smelling distance of its tether long years before this, and the shoulders of the Canadian people would have been under the staggering Grand Trunk, holding it there by a bounty of millions voted by this parliament year after year.
As for the Canadian Northern, this is a road that with greater assistance would have pulled through and been able to stand on its own feet. It is the only constituent of the whole Canadian National system that could have done so. It would have required advances beyond the advances that were given. It would have required to have been carried past the period when properly equipped, all its maintenance provided, its branch lines constructed, it would have had the traffic that would have supported a system of its mileage. B.ut it is the only one. Now they are all in the one system and the tremendous advantage of the policy that has been pursued is this, that instead of four or five, yes there would be five, unit roads each struggling and fighting with the other, each coming to this parliament year after year to be enabled to stand by itself and continue the hopeless battle, instead of such a condition as that we have all of them brought into one. We have the vast tremendous advantage of unification. We have the Grand Trunk system feeding traffic westward. We have the Canadian Northern system feeding traffic eastward. We have the Canadian Northern system turning such traffic as goes to eastern Canada through non-navigation times over to the Transcontinental railway, and we have the Transcontinental as a consequence showing this year only a trifling deficit whereas under other circumstances it would be showing a deficit to-day of millions of dollars which this parliament would have had to supply.
One word of repetition. The tremendous advantage of what has been done is not the improvement due to and flowing out of the fact that we have government operation; it is the improvement that arises from the fact that all these staggering unit systems are now one system, a system that is balanced in the east and west of Canada, a system that would be attractive to any band of capitalists

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
in the world, a system that has every hope and prospect of growing into a great success.
I want to call attention to one other fact. This system that we have was not wholly built for commercial purposes. There are long mileages of the system as respects which it was never hoped that for years at least they would be able to stand alone. If for the purposes of this discussion I may abandon all party beliefs, if one may so describe them I will refer to certain features of the system as colonization features, and not political features. Many parts of the Transcontinental, for example, a whole lot of the Grand Trunk Pacific, all of the Grand Trunk Pacific that ever should have been built, for the great part of it never should have been built, those roads are not roads that are founded on any commercial basis at all. Those roads are roads that if put on a commercial footing to be run by a private company, by any company, by any government in the world, would have waited decades after decades before they could ever stand on their feet and give a service to the country at all. Consequently, it is no more than blindness and folly to compare the results of a system so collected, of factors of so various a character-colonization, political blundering, non-commercial, all the others-it is folly to compare the results of a system so constructed, so brought together with the results of a system that was projected by business men in order that they might get business returns. So when we say that the Canadian Pacific, on the one hand, has a surplus and pays ten per cent on its capital stock, and that the Canadian National road, on the other hand, has a deficit of $51,000,000 and pays nothing on its capital stock, when we say that and believe that by saying so we are making a comparison of private ownership as against public ownership we are only talking the language of children.
Now a new board is in charge, and in charge of the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National combined. This unification took effect, so we are informed, and so the order in council discloses, on the 31st of January of this year. For the year 1923 the results will be the results of a unified system under single control, each serving the other instead of each fighting the other. We have every reason to hope for a very considerable improvement in the year 1923, a great improve- ment arising from the feature I have just recited, and arising as well from the fact that the Grand Trunk management in all its aspects is gone. Already the road has taken over its own insurance business. I quite agree, and it seems to me it is so obvious

as scarcely to need comment, that to take over its insurance business now that the two are unified is manifestly the proper course. There would be just as much reason for the government of this country insuring its own post offices all through the Dominion us for the Canadian National Railways with a business of $400,000,000 pretending to lean upon the financial strength of some insurance company. The insurance company in all probability would be weaker financially than the road itself, so the very first ingredient and primary principle of insurance would be absent.
There should, it seems to me,, be very many more economies resulting from the amalgamation. I am not a railway man, nor have I had the advantage of consultation with men who are, but I venture to say this, with a lot of deference because of the considerations I have mentioned: I venture to, say that if error is being made at this time in the reorganization because of the bringing together of the systems, it is the error of over organization rather than of simplicity. The results tabulated in the press so far would seem to indicate that an effort is being made to retain everybody possible, instead of an effort to get rid of all the overhead we can, and seek to make the system no longer top heavy. I hope I am incorrect in my diagnosis. The tremendous, almost endless, table of departments, and departmental heads,. and sub-heads, and assistants to presidents, and assistants to vice-presidents, and all sorts of door keepers and paraphernalia that has been presented to the public so far, fill me with some fear. It seems to me that we have not yet had assurance that the hand of the railway master is at work rather than the hand of the politician.
Let us have real amalgamation, and let the product of such amalgamation so appear that he who runs may read, that the wayfaring man although a fool may not err, that all the public will know the exact results year by year of the operation of the system. Before I sit down I want to impress again this thought on the minister. I do not find fault with his presentation this year, but I ask him that now, commencing with 1923, when we shall have one report rather than two, the minister present his details in tabulated form, and bring the data down to this House subsequently in blue book form, and in such array that the next year we can follow precisely in the line of the year before, that we can have parallel columns year by year, so that the eye can follow the results of an operation in each department one year with the other, so

C.N.R.-Ministers Statement
that the eye can trace a financial product year by year comparable to the year before. We have these tabulations in our own fiscal returns. We have them so presented in the Auditor General's report. We ought to have the same presentation in the financial statement of our railways so that everyone who examines it can tell at a glance just how the success of any feature of any operation, and the success of any feature of financing, compares with similar success the year before, so that we can trace through the years the ascending or descending curve illustrating the results as time goes along.
I would like the minister to take that seriously into account. The tremendous moneys involved in the operation of these railways makes it incumbent that we have each year as full and complete discussion, and as full and complete disclosure, as we have of the financial affairs of the Dominion. There should be as illuminating a debate, there should be as comprehensive a debate, and as thorough and ruthless investigation, on the presentation of the minister's statement year by year as respects the railways as we have in the annual budget debate of this House. One is of as much consequence- to the country as the- other; and I earnestly hope that some method may be found whereby-by parallel reports-not only giving the same results the year before but giving them in the same form, giving them in columns so that the eye can see the effect without much effort of the mind
that such can be done. Then the people of Canada-interested as they are in their system as their first and greatest asset-will drive politics out and drive business in by insisting on results year by year;, results that they know are improvements, and results that they can understand.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitated to get on my feet to make any remarks after the very eloquent and lucid statement we have had from the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). However, I felt that we should scarcely let this opportunity pass without complimenting the minister and the country upon the improved condition of our great National Railways. I notice that the leader of the Opposition, in commencing his remarks, could not let the opportunity pass without taking just a little hit at the Crowsnest pass agreement debate we had last year. We still feel that we were right in our attitude and that no mistake was made at that time; and any little deficit that has come to the railways through that arrangement has been fully and
amply repaid by the benefit to the people who supplied the freight on those roads.
Although' I have always believed that the only solution of our railway problem was in the national ownership of those roads, yet to-night, for the first time, I have felt almost a thrill of pride in the fact that the Canadian people really own these roads; and in the not very far distant future we are going, as the politicians say, " to point with pride " to the fact that we own that large system of railroads that we thought at one time were a millstone around the neck of the people of Canada. I am glad that we have a new board of management in whom, 1 think, the people of the country have faith; and I can only echo the words that have been repeated by the leader of the Opposition and hope that no political influences will enter into the management of this system, that these railways will have a fair chance to succeed, and that Sir Henry Thornton, and his board shall have a free field and no interference whatever in their management.
One of the things I have noticed in connection with the Canadian National Railways has been the improvement in the demeanour of the people engaged in the railway service. I think there has been a considerable improvement in the management and in the courtesy and treatment extended to passengers while travelling upon the system compared with what was experienced in these respects a few years ago. One of the things most conducive to the success of any system is when the interest and pride the people employed on it take in the service and its success. I am not going to attempt to make a speech tonight in connection with the railroads because I really do not know very much about the situation, other than that I do hope that we are on the road to prosperous times as far as our railroads are concerned. Of course, I happen to be of a rather optimistic temperament and I believe that we are going to see more prosperous times in this Dominion. With more people and more traffic, east and west, I have no fear for the future. I believe the time is not far distant when there will be no more deficits on the Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY SYSTEM (INCLUDING CENTRAL VERMONT RAILWAY)
speechtext:
(South York): I would like to draw attention to the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway, copies of which have been received by hon. members, and to point out that on page 3 there is a very succinct account of the earnings and the profits of that road for the year. In statements regarding our own railways, such

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
as the minister has presented to-day, we ought to have similar information. Then on page 14 of the same report there is a business statement of the assets and liabilities of the road. I do not say that the minister could prepare an exact statement of that kind for the use of the House at the present time, but progress in that direction could be made. Furthermore, in this Canadian Pacific Railway report there is a very succinct statement in regard to the mileage. In bur annual railway statement the number of miles of railways we own in Canada and the number of miles of railway we own in the United States, and similar information should be set forth. That has been more or less mentioned by the minister tonight, but there is no reason why we should not have the figures tabulated in our railway statement just as they are in the Canadian Pacific Railway report. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has supplied to the members of this House, and to the people of Canada, their annual statement on the lines that were referred to a few minutes ago by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). We should have information in that form; not only the figures which the minister has given to-night but an analysis of those figures somewhat in the form in which it has been prepared by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
I am one who has always believed in public ownership in this country. I see that policy coming now, and I hear almost everybody in this House saying there is no reason why it should not succeed. The greatest railway asset we have in the country to-day is the Grand Trunk. It possesses all the strategic positions in regard to traffic, or the great majority of them, in this country. It has the best grade and the best positions in the cities. It has the best position at Niagara, on the St. Lawrence, on the Detroit river, on the upper lakes, and it has good positions in cities in the West and in the West generally. There is no reason why that road, as has been said already this evening, should not be a groat asset, and should not have a surplus, instead of a deficit, in a few years. The same may be said in regard to the Canadian National. While we are speaking of our own roads, and the misadventures which they suffered, let me read to the House an item that appeared in the press this morning, in regard to the railways of the United States and the railways of Great Britain. Do hon. members know that the railways of Great Britain today are practically on the scrap heap? The railways of the United States are in a similar position, and some kind of government relief must come to those roads. I am not speaking

about the failures in connection with the railroad systems of Europe. They have all gone to pieces by reason of the war. Railways owned by the state in France, in Germany, Russia and Italy, as well as those owned by citizens, have been absolutely ruined by the war and some other things. Referring to the two cases of Great Britain and the United States, the following despatch appeared in the Ottawa press this morning:
Washington, March 26.-Enforced consolidation of United States railroads into a small number of systems putting strong and weak together, is looming up more and more as the probable big feature of the transportation recommendations which President Harding will make in his forthcoming series of speeches. This step will be urged as the only salvation for weaker roads, short of government ownership. Not improbably the British experience with consolidations which is said to have been satisfactory, will be set forth.
They have a plan in Washington, and it will be submitted to the country, to unify the roads there, and that unification will be brought about by the use of the credit of the United States and the issue of bonds. They are going to issue bonds to recover possession of the railways there. They cannot go ahead.
We have overbuilt and they have
10 p.m. underbuilt; the roads are in trouble and the government has to cqme to their relief. They are in the same position in Great Britain. A consolidation is going on there for the improvement of the railways, and the government will have to take the responsibility. So that what is coming to Canada is coming to Great Britain and the United States, and the prospect is that national ownership of railways will be more or less adopted in those countries. If that is the case, we should not be discouraged in Canada, and we should have confidence in the road and in the government, inasmuch as they have said that they intend to give government ownership a fair trial. I have not heard to-night-and I am not going to make the statement myself-that they have not given it a fair trial, and I will go so far as to congratulate the minister on the statement he made and which indicated that the railways would get a fair trial. The results of unification will come and come rapidly. We will let the public see that we really have a first-class railway system and a real solution of the railway problem in Canada.
In connection with the suggestions that have been made and the grievances which have been voiced as to our railways, the new management cannot too soon take up the question of a reclassification of freight with special reference to the basic industries that provide the great bulk of the traffic. That does not quite involve a reduction in rate, so much as

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
an improved classification. We will give advantages to the public. The public are interested in grain and the products of grain, coal and ore, and there is no reason why the new management of the National Railways should not take up reclassification and bring relief to the people of this country who are now complaining of freight rates.
I do not suggest that the new administration, or the new board of directors, should take up the question of waterways in connection with the railways, but that the parliament of Canada should immediately take up the question of the improvement of waterways and in that way help to reduce freight rates, because the nation has just as much interest in waterways as in railways. The one is complementary of the other, and there is no reason why a great reduction in freight rates cannot be effected by parliament taking up the improvement of the waterways and co-operating with the board of directors of the railways. Therefore Mr. Speaker it is a satisfaction to those who, under a great deal of discouragement, favour the nationalization of the railways, not only because of conditions that go with 'it, but because of the mess into which our railways have got, that we have public ownership to-day, and tliat it promises to be a success. The people of Canada will be more than satisfied if they find the government on its part giving public ownership a fair trial, and doing everything possible to carry out the trust confided to them.
I wish to point out that a great change has come to the railways of America by reason of the improvement of the highways and the development of the motor truck and motor car. Do hon. members know that the local passenger business of the United States, or the great bulk of it, has gone largely to the motor car? Certainly the great bulk of the local freight in the United States and in Canada now is going to the motor truck, and in that way a lot of local business has been taken from the rail-ways, and has gone to the highways and the motor car. I know districts 200 miles in extent where there are good highways, where almost all the local business in passengers and freight has gone to the motor trucks and cars operated on the highways. The great advantage of this-and we must all recognize it

is that the motor truck comes to the shipper for the freight and delivers it to the receiver. There is no cartage to pay. It goes the same day- it is taken from the shipper and there is a return /trip the next day.
The railways have suffered discouragement by the disappearance of a lot of the local business which has been profitable to them in the past. But notwithstanding all that, there is a future for the railways. There is no future for the railways th^t have not the government behind them-and that is a fact that has come out to-day-both in Britain and the United States. That being the case, we ought to have a feeling of confidence in regard to the future and of appreciation for those who put forward the idea that the only way out of the transportation problem was by government ownership, and who had not misled the country or induced it to embark upon a doubtful venture. Therefore, if the minister can improve his statements somewhat on the line of the statements given us by the Canadian Pacific Railway, we will be able to get the number of cars, the mileage, and the net receipts for the year, and we will also get, a little later on, an actual statement of the assets and liabilities in connection with these roads we have now taken over and which constitute, I hope, the greatest asset Canada has.

wages.
Has the minister the approximate amounts in lost wages? I should be glad to know what the cost of such a strike is to the country.

I have not that information, and it would be to a very large extent guess work, as I think my hon. friend will appreciate. The alleged damage to property, if any, and the loss of wages and all of these things would be mere matters of conjecture. However, I have here a memorandum that indicates the time lost and the number of men who were out of work during the year on two big coal mining strikes in Nova Scotia. In the strike from August 14 to September 5th, eighteen days, 14,353 men were out and the time lost represented 258,354 days. In district No. 18 from April 1st to August 28th, 124 days, 7,538 men were out and the time lost represented 931,960 days. The total time lost therefore was considerably over a million days.
. Mr. GUTHRIE: That is the loss in wages?
Mr. MUitDOCK: No, that is the loss of days^ and I presume that if you averaged that at $5 a day you could find the approximate total amount of money involved.

So that if I understand the matter, these strikes of which the minister has now given the particulars have cost in wages alone something between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000. If the discussion of these strikes comes properly under this item, I would ask that the item be allowed to stand until some future time, as I am aware that some hon. members desire to discuss it. Of course, if the strikes are not pertinent I have no objection to the item carrying. But when one considers the tremendous importance of these strikes to this country in view of the loss in wages to the men, the loss to the owners and operators of the mines, and the' loss to the transportation companies, one is appalled by the figures; and if the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act fails in cases of this kind, could not the minister offer some suggestion for the improvement of the act? Is there no means which this parliament could adopt which in the future would have a better effect as between the employer and the employee in the way of avoiding or settling these strikes? They run into 
untold millions, and I should think that the minister has probably given a very great deal of attention to this question. The committee would no doubt be very much pleased to know, therefore, if he can offer any practical suggestion for the improvement of the act which in future will, if possible, obviate these strikes, or some of the larger ones at all events.

The hon. member will no doubt have noted that in the proposed Bill No. 84 now before the House some suggestions are contained looking to the improvement of the act, and which it is hoped may assist in maintaining a better condition of industrial harmony. As to the question of securing a measure of any kind that will at all times, under all circumstances, guard against the possibility of a strike, or the conditions that are usually incident to a disagreement between employer and employee on vital wage questions, I regret to say that I do not believe we have come to the point where we can secure anything of that kind at present. But if my hon. friend will analyze the results that have accrued to Canada in connection with the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act he will agree that we have been remarkably fortunate, and that there has been very little loss sustained in Canada in comparison with various other countries that we might mention. I have not the slightest objection, if my hon. friend insists, to allowing this item to stand for discussion later. But I think he will concede that this particular strike in which he is interested that occurred in Sydney, Nova Scotia, in August last, was the culmination of a dispute long standing. One of the very first acts I was called upon, as Minister of Labour, to perform, was to appoint a chairman for a board that had been authorized by my predecessor in the previous government. The board was all ready to function and was just awaiting the final word to proceed. That board, as my hon. friend will recall, undertook to deal with this particular situation, with some unfortunate results for some reason or other. My hon. friend will remember also the discussion which later developed and the proposals that were made down in Sydney, with the final result that we again appointed another board in the month of April or May. That board filed its award, and that award was equally thrown to one side by {he workmen as insufficient to satisfy their demands, with the result that all at once, with very little or no notice, and in repudiation of the suggestions made in the board's award, the employees went on strike. The results therefrom are, I think, familiar to my hon. friend.
